Generated from contrib/*/results.json by python -m shortcut_detect.leaderboard build. Machine-readable copy: leaderboard.json.

docs.title: Submit a method
docs.text: A submission is one folder under contrib/ with a method.py in it. It is scored on its track's benchmark, and when the pull request is merged it is listed on the leaderboard with your name and a link to your paper. Published methods, new methods, reimplementations of other people's methods (credit them in authors) and negative results are all welcome.

docs.title: 1. Scaffold
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/criticaldata/ShortKit-ML.git && cd ShortKit-ML
uv venv --python 3.10 && source .venv/bin/activate && uv pip install -e .
python -m shortcut_detect.leaderboard new my-method --track embedding-detection

The tracks are embedding-detection, embedding-mitigation, image-detection and image-mitigation (what each one asks). The command writes contrib/my-method/method.py with the function you need to fill in and its documented inputs.

docs.title: 2. Fill in method.py
docs.text:
METADATA = {
    "name": "my-method",                 # must equal the folder name
    "title": "My Method",                # shown on the leaderboard
    "track": "embedding-detection",
    "authors": ["Ada Lovelace", "Alan Turing"],
    "paper": "https://arxiv.org/abs/...",  # optional; a list of links if several, your paper first
    "code": "https://github.com/...",      # optional, your own repository
    "description": "One sentence on the idea.",
}


def detect(embeddings, attribute, task_labels, seed=0):
    ...
    return {"score": score, "flag": p_value < 0.05}
  • One entry function per track: detect for detection tracks, fit for mitigation tracks.
  • Use seed for every random choice; the benchmark checks that scores reproduce.
  • Helper modules next to method.py can be imported normally.
  • Extra packages go in contrib/my-method/requirements.txt; CI installs them. Keep them pip-installable on CPU.
  • Keep your method's own cost modest. A full scoring run on an embedding track takes minutes. A full run on an image track takes longer, because the benchmark trains the small shared CNN once per dataset (22 datasets for image detection, 6 settings plus their ERM references for image mitigation), and that alone can take well over half an hour on a laptop CPU. Use validate while developing; it runs the quick suite.
  • The method may wrap code that lives in your own repository (installed through requirements.txt): the folder only needs the adapter.

docs.title: 3. Check and score
docs.text:
python -m shortcut_detect.leaderboard validate contrib/my-method   # quick suite, about a minute
python -m shortcut_detect.leaderboard score contrib/my-method      # full suite, writes results.json
python -m shortcut_detect.leaderboard build                         # updates the leaderboard page

Commit method.py, results.json, any helpers, and the updated docs/leaderboard/.

docs.title: 4. Open a pull request
docs.text:
Use the method submission checklist in the pull request template. CI then

  1. validates METADATA and runs your method on the quick suite,
  2. rescores it on the full suite and checks that the numbers match your results.json, and
  3. posts the scores in the run summary, next to the current leaders of your track.

Scores are reproduced on the CI runner, not on your machine. Methods built on numpy and scikit-learn usually match to the last digit everywhere. Methods that train with torch, and everything on the image tracks (which train a CNN), can come out differently on another operating system or processor even with the same seed. If step 2 fails only because of that, download the scored-results-<track> artifact from the CI run, replace your results.json with the one in it, and push. The leaderboard lists the scores CI computed. CI uses the package versions in uv.lock, Python 3.11 and CPU-only torch.

A maintainer reviews the code before merging: CI runs your code, so the review checks it does nothing beyond the method (no network calls, no reading files outside its folder). Once merged, the leaderboard on the docs site updates with the next deploy.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• No peeking. Methods may not read the benchmark's generator internals (planted dimensions, patch corner, rho) or special-case the seeds. Column order and patch position are randomized per dataset for that reason, and maintainers rescore entries on fresh seeds (score --seed-offset) before a benchmark release; an entry whose ranking only holds on the public seeds is removed.
  • Detection tracks see no answers. Embedding detection gets the attribute (the question is whether the embedding carries it beyond the label); image detection gets no attribute labels at all.
  • Mitigation tracks may use group labels on the training set, as most published mitigation methods do. Methods that do not need them are noted in description.
  • One entry per method. Variants with different hyperparameters belong in one folder with the settings you recommend. A substantially different method gets its own folder.
  • Stale scores. When a track's benchmark version changes, older results on that track are shown as stale until they are rescored; maintainers rescore baselines and ask authors about the rest.
  • Flags must mean something. On detection tracks, an entry whose flag fires on more than 20% of null datasets ranks below every entry whose flag does not, whatever its AUROC (details).

docs.title: Not ready to write code?
docs.text: Open a method proposal issue with the paper and a reference implementation, and the community or the maintainers can port it, with you credited as an author.

docs.title: Tracks
docs.text:
All data is generated from seeds by the package itself, so there is nothing to download and no licensed data is involved. Every metric is higher-is-better except FPR and residual leakage.

Each track has its own benchmark version (TRACKS[key].version), so changing one track's suite only marks that track's results stale:

Track Version Changes embedding-detection 1.1 30 null datasets per variant instead of 10 embedding-mitigation 1.0 image-detection 1.0 image-mitigation 1.0

docs.title: Ranking the detection tracks
docs.text:
A detection entry returns a continuous score and, optionally, a yes/no flag. The score is ranked by AUROC, which says nothing about the flag: a detector whose flag fires on every dataset can still order its scores well. So on both detection tracks the table is ordered in three groups, each by AUROC:

  1. entries whose flag fires on at most 20% of null datasets (shortcut_detect.leaderboard.MAX_FLAG_FPR),
  2. entries that return no flag,
  3. entries whose flag fires on more than 20% of null datasets, marked flag FPR > 0.2.

A flag at a nominal α = 0.05 stays well under the cap. Leaving the flag out cannot lift an entry above one whose flag is calibrated.

docs.title: embedding-detection
docs.text:
Question. Do embeddings E carry an attribute A beyond what the task label Y explains?

Data. shortcut_detect.benchmark.conditional_synthetic.generate_conditional_synthetic with n = 600, 64 dimensions, A agreeing with Y 70% of the time, 4 task dimensions and 4 attribute dimensions, columns shuffled per dataset. The attribute signal has strength δ ∈ {0 (null), 0.3, 0.6, 1.0} and one of three forms:

Variant How A is carried What it rewards linear mean shift of δ standard deviations the easy case xor sign of the product of dimension pairs; no mean difference non-linear detectors variance equal means, standard deviation 1 + δ in one group detectors beyond the mean

Null datasets (δ = 0) still have A correlated with Y, so E predicts A through the task dimensions. A method that ignores Y fires on them.

Suite. Per variant, 10 seeds for each of the three strengths δ ∈ {0.3, 0.6, 1.0} and 30 null seeds (δ = 0), so nulls and shortcut datasets are equal in number: 3 × 60 = 180 datasets (quick: 2 seeds each). Version 1.0 had 10 nulls per variant; with that few, a per-variant AUROC moved by about ±0.15 from seed noise alone. Even with 30, a method that cannot see a variant scores 0.5 ± 0.075 (one standard deviation) on it, so read a per-variant AUROC well under 0.5 as "blind to this variant", not as worse than chance. For example, the conditional probe is linear and cannot see the XOR signal: it scores 0.41 on the public XOR seeds (0.31 under version 1.0) and 0.55–0.59 on four sets of fresh seeds.

Entry. detect(embeddings, attribute, task_labels, seed) -> float | {"score", "flag"}.

Metrics. auroc: how well the score separates shortcut from null datasets, averaged over the three variants (ranking metric, after the flag groups); per-variant AUROC. With a flag: fpr on nulls (should be near your nominal α), tpr on shortcut datasets, and tpr_delta_* by strength.

docs.title: embedding-mitigation
docs.text:
Question. Can you train a task classifier that does not lean on the attribute?

Data. Linear variant, 64 dimensions, task effect 0.8. Training: n = 2000 with A agreeing with Y at rho ∈ {0.9, 0.97}, attribute strength δ ∈ {1, 2}. Test: n = 4000 with rho = 0.5, so the attribute says nothing about the label. 4 settings × 5 seeds (quick: 1 seed).

Entry. fit(embeddings, attribute, task_labels, seed) returning an object with predict(embeddings); optionally transform(embeddings).

Metrics. worst_group_acc: test accuracy of the worst of the four (task, attribute) groups, averaged over settings (ranking metric); mean_acc over the groups; gain_over_erm, the worst-group gain over plain logistic regression on the same split; with transform, leakage_auroc, the out-of-fold AUROC of a probe predicting A from [transform(E), Y] on the test set (0.5 = nothing left).

docs.title: image-detection
docs.text:
Question. Does a trained model rely on a hidden shortcut, and where is it?

Data. 32×32 RGB images of one faint bar, horizontal or vertical (the task), on a noisy background. The shortcut is a 4×4 red patch in one corner; the corner is fixed within a dataset and chosen by its seed. The patch agrees with the label with probability rho ∈ {0.9, 0.95, 0.98, 1.0} (shortcut-trained) or 0.5 (null datasets: the patch is in half the images but carries no information). For each dataset the shared CNN is trained on 1500 images; the method gets 400 held-out images, their labels and the trained model, and no attribute labels. Seeds per strength: 9 nulls; 3, 2 and 2 at rho 0.9, 0.95 and 0.98; 6 at rho 1.0 (quick: 2 nulls, one each at 0.9 and 1.0).

Ground truth is measured, not assumed. The training rho does not decide whether a given model actually uses the patch: at rho 0.9 one seed may lean on it and another not. So for every dataset the benchmark computes the model's reliance: the share of patched held-out images whose prediction changes when the patch is painted gray. A shortcut-trained dataset counts as a shortcut case when reliance ≥ 0.2, and as ambiguous otherwise. Below rho 1 the shared CNN usually learns the bar and leans on the patch only a little, so most clear shortcut cases come from rho 1; the partial strengths mostly test whether a score tracks how much the model relies on the patch. Null datasets are always nulls. Each dataset's rho, reliance and label are in details.per_dataset of results.json.

Entry. detect(images, task_labels, model, seed) -> float | {"score", "flag", "heatmaps"} with images of shape (n, 3, 32, 32) in [0, 1] and heatmaps of shape (n, 32, 32).

Metrics. auroc of the score, shortcut vs null datasets, ambiguous ones left out (ranking metric, after the flag groups); reliance_spearman: rank correlation between the score and the measured reliance over all datasets, ambiguous included (does the score track how much the model relies on the patch?); with heatmaps, pointing_game: share of patched images in shortcut datasets whose heatmap peak falls on the patch (within 2 pixels); with a flag, fpr on nulls and tpr on shortcut cases.

docs.title: image-mitigation
docs.text:
Question. Can you train an image classifier that ignores the patch?

Data. The same images. Training: n = 2000 with the patch agreeing with the label at rho ∈ {0.9, 0.97}. Test: n = 2000 with rho = 0.5. 2 settings × 3 seeds (quick: 1 seed). Trained without a usable patch (rho = 0.5) the shared CNN reached about 0.77 worst-group accuracy in our runs, a rough ceiling for this backbone and budget.

Entry. fit(images, attribute, task_labels, seed) returning an object with predict(images).

Metrics. worst_group_acc (ranking metric), mean_acc, gain_over_erm against the shared CNN trained with plain cross-entropy.

docs.title: Shared CNN
docs.text: shortcut_detect.leaderboard.image_models.make_cnn(): three 3×3 conv blocks (16, 32, 64 channels, BatchNorm, ReLU, max-pool after the first two), global average pooling and a linear head; train_classifier() trains it with Adam (lr 3e-3, batch 64, 8 epochs) on optionally weighted cross-entropy. Mitigation methods may use any model, but using this one keeps the comparison about the method.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: The committed scores are the ones computed on the CI runner (submitting). Embedding-detection scores reproduce exactly (verify tolerance 1e-6). Embedding-mitigation scores are checked with a tolerance of 0.01 and image-track scores with 0.02: entries that train with PyTorch can move slightly between CPU models (by about 0.002 for the contrastive encoder), even on the CI runners. Scores on fresh seeds: python -m shortcut_detect.leaderboard score contrib/<name> --seed-offset 1.

docs.title: Adversarial Debiasing (M04)
docs.text: Adversarial Debiasing is a model-level mitigation (Zhang et al. 2018) that uses adversarial training to remove demographic encoding from embeddings. The encoder learns representations that predict the task while being uninformative for the protected attribute, via a Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL).

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Zhang, B. H., Lemoine, B., & Mitchell, M. (2018). Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning. AIES 2018. The predictor and adversary are trained jointly so the predictor remains accurate while exhibiting less stereotyping.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
• Input: Embeddings, protected (demographic) labels, and optionally task labels.
  • Training: Encoder maps embeddings to a hidden representation. An adversary tries to predict the protected attribute from this representation via a GRL. The encoder learns to minimize task loss while maximizing adversary loss (making protected attribute unpredictable).
  • Output: Debiased embeddings with reduced demographic encoding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• PyTorch (already a dependency of shortkit-ml).
  • NumPy.

docs.title: Without task labels (demographic removal only)
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import AdversarialDebiasing, SKLearnProbe
import numpy as np

# Embeddings (n_samples, embed_dim) and protected labels (e.g., gender)
embeddings = ...  # shape (N, D)
protected_labels = ...  # shape (N,), e.g., 0/1 for binary

debiaser = AdversarialDebiasing(
    hidden_dim=64,
    adversary_weight=0.5,
    n_epochs=50,
    batch_size=64,
    random_state=42,
)
debiaser.fit(embeddings, protected_labels)
embeddings_debiased = debiaser.transform(embeddings)
# embeddings_debiased has shape (N, hidden_dim)

docs.title: With task labels (preserve utility)
docs.text:
debiaser = AdversarialDebiasing(
    hidden_dim=64,
    adversary_weight=0.5,
    n_epochs=50,
)
debiaser.fit(embeddings, protected_labels, task_labels=task_labels)
embeddings_debiased = debiaser.transform(embeddings)

docs.title: Verify debiasing
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import SKLearnProbe

probe = SKLearnProbe(threshold=0.7)
probe.fit(embeddings, protected_labels)
acc_before = probe.metric_value_

probe.fit(embeddings_debiased, protected_labels)
acc_after = probe.metric_value_

print(f"Probe accuracy before: {acc_before:.2%}")
print(f"Probe accuracy after: {acc_after:.2%}")  # Should drop significantly

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• hidden_dim: Hidden dimension of the encoder (default: min(64, embed_dim)).
  • adversary_weight: Weight for adversarial loss; higher removes more demographic info (default 0.5).
  • n_epochs: Training epochs (default 50).
  • batch_size: Batch size (default 64).
  • lr: Learning rate (default 1e-3).
  • dropout: Dropout rate in encoder (default 0.1).
  • random_state: Seed for reproducibility.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Run detection (e.g., Probe) to confirm demographic encoding.
  2. Fit AdversarialDebiasing on embeddings and protected labels.
  3. Use transform() to obtain debiased embeddings for downstream tasks.
  4. Re-run Probe to verify reduced demographic predictability.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Probe or geometric analysis indicates high demographic encoding.
  • You need model-level mitigation (vs. data augmentation like M01/M02).
  • You want to retain task utility while removing demographic information.

docs.title: Background Randomization (M02)
docs.text: Background Randomization is a data mitigation approach (Kwon et al. 2023) that swaps foregrounds with random backgrounds across samples. This breaks spurious object–background correlations so models cannot rely on background shortcuts.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Kwon et al. (ICLR 2023): "Disentangled Feature Swapping Augmentation for Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation." A pixel-level approximation composes new images by pasting the foreground (masked region) of one image onto the background of another.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: Given images and foreground masks, for each sample i the method picks a random sample j (j != i) and produces: augmented_i = background_j + foreground_i. The foreground of image i is pasted onto the background of image j.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: NumPy and PIL only. No extra dependencies.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import BackgroundRandomizer
import numpy as np

randomizer = BackgroundRandomizer(augment_fraction=1.0, random_state=42)
# images: (N, H, W) or (N, H, W, C), values in [0, 1]
# foreground_masks: (N, H, W), 1 = foreground, 0 = background
augmented = randomizer.swap_foregrounds(images, foreground_masks)

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
In the Advanced Analysis tab, use the Background Randomization (M02) accordion:

  • Upload images and either foreground mask images or a heatmap file (.npz/.npy).
  • Set heatmap threshold and augment fraction.
  • Download a zip of augmented images.

Requires at least 2 images to perform swaps.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Obtain foreground masks (from GradCAM, segmentation model, or manual annotation).
  2. Run Background Randomization to produce augmented images.
  3. Use the augmented data for retraining.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• augment_fraction: Fraction of samples to augment, 0–1 (default 1.0).
  • random_state: Seed for reproducible randomization.

docs.title: Embedding Bias Direction (PCA)
docs.text: This method extracts a bias direction from group prototypes using PCA and measures the projection gap across groups. Large gaps indicate systematic embedding bias.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.geometric import BiasDirectionPCADetector

detector = BiasDirectionPCADetector()
detector.fit(embeddings, group_labels)
print(detector.report_)

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• projection_gap: max–min projection across groups
  • explained_variance: variance explained by the bias direction
  • group_projections: per-group projection means and support

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Bolukbasi et al. 2016: https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06520

docs.title: Causal Effect Regularization
docs.text: Causal Effect Regularization (Kumar et al., 2023) estimates the causal effect of each attribute on the task label. Attributes with near-zero estimated effect are flagged as spurious shortcuts.

docs.title: What It Detects
docs.text:
• Per-attribute causal effect on the task label.
  • Attributes with low causal effect (spurious) that the classifier should not rely on.

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text:
• embeddings: np.ndarray (n, d) representation space
  • labels: np.ndarray (n,) task labels
  • attributes: dict[str, np.ndarray] - attribute name -> (n,) values per sample (binary or categorical)

Optional:

  • counterfactual_pairs: For interventional data (Phase 2). Not used in current Direct estimator.

docs.title: Unified API Example
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector

loader = {
    "embeddings": emb,
    "labels": labels,
    "attributes": {
        "race": race_labels,
        "color": color_labels,
    },
}

detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=["causal_effect"],
    causal_effect_spurious_threshold=0.1,
)
detector.fit_from_loaders({"causal_effect": loader})

result = detector.get_results()["causal_effect"]
print(result["metrics"])
print(result["report"]["per_attribute"])

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• Attributes with |TE_a| < threshold are flagged as spurious (shortcuts).
  • Higher estimated causal effect indicates the attribute may be task-relevant.
  • Risk levels:
  • high: multiple spurious attributes
  • moderate: one spurious attribute
  • low: no spurious attributes

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Kumar, Abhinav, Amit Deshpande, and Amit Sharma. "Causal Effect Regularization: Automated Detection and Removal of Spurious Attributes." arXiv:2306.11072 (2023).

docs.title: CAV (Concept Activation Vectors)
docs.text:
Concept Activation Vectors (Kim et al., 2018) test whether model representations encode human-interpretable shortcut concepts.

This implementation focuses on precomputed activations and optional directional derivatives (for TCAV scoring), which fits the library's loader-driven XAI workflow.

docs.title: What It Detects
docs.text:
• Whether a concept is linearly separable from a random baseline in activation space.
  • Whether model sensitivity aligns with that concept direction (TCAV score).

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text:
• concept_sets: dict[str, np.ndarray] where each array is (n, d)
  • random_set: np.ndarray (n, d) or list of arrays

Optional:

  • target_activations: np.ndarray (m, d)
  • target_directional_derivatives: np.ndarray (m, d)

If directional derivatives are omitted, TCAV risk is reported as unknown.

docs.title: Unified API Example
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector

bundle = {
    "concept_sets": {
        "hospital_token": concept_arr,  # (n,d)
        "device_artifact": artifact_arr,
    },
    "random_set": random_arr,  # (n,d)
    "target_activations": target_acts,  # optional
    "target_directional_derivatives": target_dd,  # optional
}

detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=["cav"],
    cav_quality_threshold=0.7,
    cav_shortcut_threshold=0.6,
)
detector.fit_from_loaders({"cav": bundle})

result = detector.get_results()["cav"]
print(result["metrics"])
print(result["report"]["per_concept"])

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• High concept quality (AUC) + high TCAV indicates likely shortcut reliance.
  • A concept is flagged when both thresholds are exceeded.
  • Risk levels:
  • high: very strong flagged TCAV signal
  • moderate: flagged concepts, weaker maximum signal
  • low: tested with derivatives, no flagged concepts
  • unknown: derivatives not provided

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Kim, Been, et al. "Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)." ICML 2018.

docs.title: Contrastive Debiasing (M07)
docs.text: Contrastive Debiasing is a model-level mitigation (Zhang et al. 2022, Correct-n-Contrast) that uses contrastive learning to separate shortcuts from task-relevant signals. Same-class examples with different spurious (group) attributes are pulled together; different-class examples are pushed apart.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Zhang, R., Sharma, A., Li, J., Chen, S., Wang, Y., & Ré, C. (2022). Correct-N-Contrast: A Contrastive Approach for Improving Robustness to Spurious Correlations. ICML 2022. Contrastive learning with anchor-positive-negative sampling improves worst-group accuracy without requiring group labels at inference.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
• Input: Embeddings, task labels, and group (protected/spurious) labels.
  • Training: Anchors are from a (task, group) slice. Positives = same task, different group. Negatives = different task. InfoNCE contrastive loss + optional CE for task preservation. Encoder learns representations invariant to group while preserving task signal.
  • Output: Debiased embeddings with reduced spurious encoding.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• PyTorch (already a dependency of shortkit-ml).
  • NumPy.
  • At least 2 task classes and 2 groups (each task must have samples in at least 2 groups).

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ContrastiveDebiasing, SKLearnProbe
import numpy as np

# Embeddings (n_samples, embed_dim), task labels, and group labels
embeddings = ...  # shape (N, D)
task_labels = ...  # shape (N,), e.g., 0/1 for binary task
group_labels = ...  # shape (N,), e.g., 0/1 for binary spurious attribute

cnc = ContrastiveDebiasing(
    hidden_dim=32,
    temperature=0.05,
    contrastive_weight=0.75,
    use_task_loss=True,
    n_epochs=50,
    batch_size=64,
    random_state=42,
)
cnc.fit(embeddings, task_labels, group_labels)
embeddings_debiased = cnc.transform(embeddings)
# embeddings_debiased has shape (N, hidden_dim)

docs.title: Verify debiasing
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import SKLearnProbe

probe = SKLearnProbe(threshold=0.7)
probe.fit(embeddings, group_labels)
acc_before = probe.metric_value_

probe.fit(embeddings_debiased, group_labels)
acc_after = probe.metric_value_

print(f"Probe accuracy before: {acc_before:.2%}")
print(f"Probe accuracy after: {acc_after:.2%}")  # Should drop significantly

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• hidden_dim: Hidden dimension of the encoder (default: min(64, embed_dim)).
  • temperature: Temperature for InfoNCE contrastive loss; lower = sharper (default 0.05).
  • contrastive_weight: Weight for contrastive loss vs CE; 1.0 = pure contrastive (default 0.75).
  • use_task_loss: If True, jointly minimize CE for task prediction (default True).
  • n_epochs: Training epochs (default 50).
  • batch_size: Batch size (default 64).
  • lr: Learning rate (default 1e-3).
  • dropout: Dropout rate in encoder (default 0.1).
  • random_state: Seed for reproducibility.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Run detection (e.g., Probe) to confirm spurious encoding.
  2. Fit ContrastiveDebiasing on embeddings, task labels, and group labels.
  3. Use transform() to obtain debiased embeddings for downstream tasks.
  4. Re-run Probe on group labels to verify reduced spurious predictability.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Probe or geometric analysis indicates strong spurious/group encoding.
  • You have both task and group labels.
  • You want model-level mitigation that aligns same-class/different-group representations.
  • Correct-n-Contrast is suited for worst-group robustness when spurious correlations exist.

docs.title: Demographic Parity Detector
docs.text: Demographic Parity measures the difference in positive prediction rates across demographic groups. A large gap indicates that the model's predictions depend on group membership, which may signal shortcut reliance on protected or spurious attributes.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Train a logistic regression probe on embeddings vs. task labels
  2. Predict labels using the trained probe
  3. Compute positive prediction rates per demographic group
  4. Calculate the DP gap: max rate minus min rate across groups
  5. Assess risk by comparing the gap to a configurable threshold
graph TD
    A[Embeddings + Labels + Group Labels] --> B[Train Logistic Regression]
    B --> C[Predict Labels]
    C --> D[Compute Per-Group Positive Rates]
    D --> E[DP Gap = Max Rate - Min Rate]
    E --> F{Gap >= Threshold?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Shortcut Detected]
    F -->|No| H[No Shortcut Detected]

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.fairness import DemographicParityDetector

detector = DemographicParityDetector(
    dp_gap_threshold=0.1,
    min_group_size=10,
)

detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels=group_labels)
report = detector.get_report()

print(f"Shortcut detected: {report['shortcut_detected']}")
print(f"Risk level: {report['risk_level']}")
print(f"DP gap: {report['metrics']['dp_gap']:.3f}")

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description estimator LogisticRegression None Optional sklearn classifier (default: LogisticRegression with max_iter=1000) min_group_size int 10 Minimum group size; smaller groups get NaN rates dp_gap_threshold float 0.1 Gap threshold for flagging shortcut risk

docs.title: Report Structure
docs.text: Field Type Description shortcut_detected bool Whether the DP gap exceeds the threshold risk_level str "low", "moderate", "high", or "unknown" metrics.dp_gap float Max minus min positive prediction rate across groups metrics.overall_positive_rate float Overall positive prediction rate report.group_rates dict Per-group positive rate and support

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Risk Level Condition Low DP gap < threshold Moderate DP gap >= threshold High DP gap >= 2x threshold Unknown Insufficient data to assess

docs.title: Example with Synthetic Data
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from shortcut_detect.fairness import DemographicParityDetector

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 400

# Two demographic groups with different embedding distributions
embeddings = rng.standard_normal((n, 16))
labels = np.array([0] * 200 + [1] * 200)
group_labels = np.array([0] * 100 + [1] * 100 + [0] * 100 + [1] * 100)

# Inject bias: group 1 has a spurious signal correlated with label
embeddings[100:200, 0] += 2.0
embeddings[300:400, 0] += 2.0

detector = DemographicParityDetector(dp_gap_threshold=0.1)
detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels=group_labels)

report = detector.get_report()
print(f"Shortcut detected: {report['shortcut_detected']}")
print(f"DP gap: {report['metrics']['dp_gap']:.3f}")

docs.title: Unified API Integration
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector

detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=["demographic_parity"],
    seed=42,
)
detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels=group_labels)
print(detector.summary())

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use Demographic Parity Detector when:

  • You have demographic or protected group labels
  • You want to measure fairness of predictions across groups
  • You need a standard fairness metric (Feldman et al. 2015)
  • Your task has binary labels

Don't use Demographic Parity Detector when:

  • You do not have group labels (use GCE or Probe-based detection instead)
  • Your task has more than two classes (requires binary labels)
  • Groups are too small (fewer than min_group_size samples each)

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
Demographic parity requires that the positive prediction rate is equal across groups:

$$P(\hat{Y} = 1 \mid G = g) = P(\hat{Y} = 1) \quad \forall g$$

The DP gap measures the maximum deviation:

$$\text{DP Gap} = \max_g P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid G=g) - \min_g P(\hat{Y}=1 \mid G=g)$$

A large DP gap suggests the model's predictions are influenced by group membership, potentially through shortcut features correlated with the protected attribute.

Reference: Feldman et al. 2015, "Certifying and Removing Disparate Impact."

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Equalized Odds - Complementary fairness metric
  • GCE Detector - Sample-level minority detection
  • API Reference - Full API documentation
  • Overview - Compare all methods

docs.title: Early-Epoch Clustering (SPARE)
docs.text: Early-epoch clustering detects shortcut bias by exploiting the tendency of SGD-trained models to learn simple (often spurious) features early in training. By clustering representations or logits from the first few epochs, we can identify imbalanced clusters that suggest shortcut reliance.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• You can capture early-epoch representations (logits or features).
  • You lack protected-group labels but want a proxy signal.
  • You want a training-time shortcut signal before full convergence.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.training import EarlyEpochClusteringDetector

# early_epoch_reps: array of shape (n_samples, n_features)
# labels optional; used only for cluster-label agreement

detector = EarlyEpochClusteringDetector(
    n_clusters=4,
    min_cluster_ratio=0.1,
    entropy_threshold=0.7,
)

detector.fit(early_epoch_reps, labels=labels, n_epochs=1)
print(detector.report_)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• Low entropy / low minority ratio → clusters are imbalanced, suggesting shortcut bias.
  • High entropy / balanced clusters → no strong shortcut signal detected.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Yang et al. 2023, SPARE (SePArate early and REsample).

docs.title: Equalized Odds (Fairness Analysis)
docs.text:
Equalized Odds detects shortcuts by measuring True Positive Rate (TPR) and False Positive Rate (FPR) disparities across protected groups.

Based on Hardt et al. (2016), this method checks whether a classifier trained on embeddings satisfies the equalized odds criterion: equal TPR and FPR across all demographic groups.

Large gaps indicate that the embeddings encode group-dependent shortcuts that cause differential performance.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The Equalized Odds detector:

  1. Trains a lightweight classifier (LogisticRegression by default) on embeddings to predict task labels
  2. Computes per-group metrics: TPR and FPR for each protected group
  3. Calculates gaps: gap = max(rate) - min(rate) across groups
  4. Assesses risk based on gap thresholds
graph TD
    A[Embeddings + Labels + Groups] --> B[Train Classifier]
    B --> C[Predictions]
    C --> D[Per-Group TPR/FPR]
    D --> E[Compute Gaps]
    E --> F{Gap >= Threshold?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Shortcut Detected]
    F -->|No| H[No Shortcut]

Key insight: If TPR or FPR differs significantly across groups, the model treats groups unequally for the same ground truth, suggesting shortcut reliance.

docs.title: Via the Unified API (Recommended)
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector
import numpy as np

# Precomputed embeddings
embeddings = np.load("embeddings.npy")
labels = np.load("labels.npy")  # Binary labels required
group_labels = np.load("groups.npy")  # Required

detector = ShortcutDetector(methods=["equalized_odds"])
detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels=group_labels)

print(detector.summary())

docs.title: Standalone Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.fairness import EqualizedOddsDetector

detector = EqualizedOddsDetector(
    tpr_gap_threshold=0.1,
    fpr_gap_threshold=0.1,
    min_group_size=10,
)

detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels)

print(f"TPR Gap: {detector.tpr_gap_:.3f}")
print(f"FPR Gap: {detector.fpr_gap_:.3f}")
print(f"Risk Level: {detector.report_.risk_level}")

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description estimator Estimator LogisticRegression Classifier to train on embeddings min_group_size int 10 Minimum samples per group (smaller groups get NaN) tpr_gap_threshold float 0.1 Threshold for flagging TPR disparity fpr_gap_threshold float 0.1 Threshold for flagging FPR disparity

docs.title: Report Structure
docs.text:
results_["equalized_odds"]["report"] contains an EqualizedOddsReport:

Field Type Description group_metrics dict Per-group TPR, FPR, support, and confusion matrix counts tpr_gap float Max TPR - Min TPR across groups fpr_gap float Max FPR - Min FPR across groups overall_accuracy float Classifier accuracy on all samples risk_level str "low", "moderate", or "high" notes str Human-readable interpretation reference str "Hardt et al. 2016"

docs.title: Per-Group Metrics
docs.text:
For each group, group_metrics[group_id] contains:

Metric Description tpr True Positive Rate = TP / (TP + FN) fpr False Positive Rate = FP / (FP + TN) support Number of samples in the group tp, fp, tn, fn Confusion matrix counts

docs.title: Risk Assessment
docs.text: Risk Level Condition Interpretation Low Both gaps < threshold Equalized odds approximately satisfied Moderate Any gap >= threshold Noticeable disparity in TPR or FPR High Any gap >= 2x threshold Large disparity, strong evidence of shortcuts

docs.title: What the Metrics Mean
docs.text:
Pattern Interpretation High TPR gap Model catches positives better for some groups than others High FPR gap Model makes more false alarms for some groups Both gaps high Systematic unfairness across both error types Low accuracy + low gaps Fair but poorly performing model

Rule of thumb

If TPR or FPR differs by more than 10% across groups, the embeddings likely encode shortcuts correlated with group membership.

docs.title: Example with Synthetic Data
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(42)

# Create embeddings where group 0 has stronger signal
n = 500
embeddings = np.random.randn(n, 20)
labels = (embeddings[:, 0] > 0).astype(int)
groups = np.array([0] * 250 + [1] * 250)

# Add shortcut: group 1 has noisier signal
embeddings[250:, 0] += np.random.randn(250) * 2

detector = ShortcutDetector(methods=["equalized_odds"])
detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels=groups)

print(detector.summary())

Expected: Higher TPR/FPR gaps due to differential signal quality across groups.

docs.title: When to Use Equalized Odds
docs.text:
Use Equalized Odds when:

  • You have binary task labels (required)
  • You have explicit group labels (demographics, environments)
  • You want interpretable fairness metrics
  • You need to report regulatory fairness compliance
  • You want to measure differential error rates across groups

Don't use Equalized Odds when:

  • Labels are multi-class (use other methods)
  • Group labels are unavailable
  • You want unsupervised detection (use HBAC, Geometric)
  • Groups are too small (< 10 samples each)

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
Equalized Odds (Hardt et al., 2016) requires:

$$ P(\hat{Y}=1 | Y=y, A=a) = P(\hat{Y}=1 | Y=y, A=a') $$

For all $y \in {0, 1}$ and protected groups $a, a'$.

This decomposes into two constraints:

  • Equal TPR: $P(\hat{Y}=1 | Y=1, A=a) = P(\hat{Y}=1 | Y=1, A=a')$
  • Equal FPR: $P(\hat{Y}=1 | Y=0, A=a) = P(\hat{Y}=1 | Y=0, A=a')$

The detector measures violations as:

$$ \text{TPR Gap} = \max_a \text{TPR}_a - \min_a \text{TPR}_a $$

$$ \text{FPR Gap} = \max_a \text{FPR}_a - \min_a \text{FPR}_a $$

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• GroupDRO - Worst-group performance analysis
  • Probe-based Detection - Predictability of group attributes
  • Statistical Tests - Feature-wise group differences
  • Overview - Comparing all detection methods

docs.title: Explanation Regularization (M05 RRR)
docs.text: Explanation Regularization (Right for Right Reasons, RRR) is a model-level mitigation (Ross et al. 2017) that penalizes input gradients on shortcut regions during training. The model is discouraged from relying on irrelevant features for predictions.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Ross, A. S., Hughes, M. C., & Doshi-Velez, F. (2017). Right for the Right Reasons: Training Differentiable Models by Constraining their Explanations. IJCAI 2017. arXiv:1703.03717

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
• Input: PyTorch model, images, task labels, shortcut masks (or heatmap file).
  • Training: For each batch, compute task loss (cross-entropy) plus a penalty on input gradients weighted by the shortcut mask: L = L_task + λ * Σ(mask ⊙ (∂log p(y|x)/∂x)²).
  • Output: Fine-tuned model checkpoint (.pt).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• PyTorch (already a dependency of shortkit-ml).
  • Model must be differentiable end-to-end.
  • Shortcut regions must be identified (e.g., via GradCAM, expert annotation).

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ExplanationRegularization
import torch
import numpy as np

# model, images (N,C,H,W), labels (N,), shortcut_masks (N,H,W) with 1=shortcut
model = ...
images = torch.randn(32, 3, 224, 224)
labels = np.array([0, 1] * 16)
masks = np.random.rand(32, 224, 224)  # 1 where shortcut

rrr = ExplanationRegularization(
    lambda_rrr=1.0,
    lr=1e-4,
    n_epochs=10,
    batch_size=8,
    head="logits",
    random_state=42,
)
rrr.fit(model, images, labels, masks)
# model is updated in-place

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• lambda_rrr: Weight for gradient penalty (default 1.0).
  • lr: Learning rate (default 1e-4).
  • n_epochs: Training epochs (default 10).
  • batch_size: Batch size (default 8).
  • head: How to extract logits from model output, e.g. "logits" or 0 (default "logits").
  • random_state: Seed for reproducibility.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Run detection (e.g., GradCAM mask overlap) to identify shortcut regions.
  2. Create shortcut masks (1 on shortcut, 0 elsewhere).
  3. Fit ExplanationRegularization with model, images, labels, and masks.
  4. Use the fine-tuned model for inference.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• GradCAM or SpRAy indicates the model attends to shortcut regions.
  • You have model access and can fine-tune.
  • You want to steer the model toward the right features without retraining from scratch.

docs.title: Frequency Detector
docs.text: Embedding-space frequency shortcut detector detects whether class signals are overly concentrated in a small set of embedding dimensions. It does not localize input-domain frequency artifacts (e.g., image Fourier bands). Instead, it identifies representational shortcut signatures from class-separable dimensions.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Train a probe (logistic regression by default) on embeddings vs. task labels
  2. Predict labels using the probe (on training data or a holdout split)
  3. Compute per-class TPR/FPR from the probe predictions
  4. Flag shortcut classes where TPR >= threshold AND FPR <= threshold
  5. Extract top-k dimensions from the probe coefficient magnitudes
  6. Assess risk based on the fraction of flagged classes
graph TD
    A[Embeddings + Labels] --> B[Train Logistic Probe]
    B --> C[Predict Labels]
    C --> D[Compute Per-Class TPR/FPR]
    D --> E{TPR >= threshold AND FPR <= threshold?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Flag as Shortcut Class]
    E -->|No| G[Not a Shortcut Class]
    F --> H[Extract Top-k Dimensions]
    H --> I[Assess Risk Level]
    G --> I

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import FrequencyDetector

detector = FrequencyDetector(
    top_percent=0.05,
    tpr_threshold=0.5,
    fpr_threshold=0.15,
    probe_evaluation="holdout",
    probe_holdout_frac=0.2,
)

detector.fit(embeddings, labels)
report = detector.get_report()

print(f"Shortcut detected: {report['shortcut_detected']}")
print(f"Risk level: {report['risk_level']}")
print(f"Shortcut classes: {report['report']['shortcut_classes']}")

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description top_percent float 0.05 Fraction of top embedding dimensions to examine tpr_threshold float 0.5 Per-class true-positive-rate threshold for shortcut flagging fpr_threshold float 0.15 Per-class false-positive-rate threshold for shortcut flagging probe_estimator BaseEstimator None Optional sklearn classifier (default: LogisticRegression) probe_evaluation str "train" Evaluation mode: "train" or "holdout" probe_holdout_frac float 0.2 Holdout fraction when probe_evaluation="holdout" random_state int 42 Random seed for reproducibility

docs.title: Report Structure
docs.text: Field Type Description shortcut_detected bool Whether any class was flagged risk_level str "low", "moderate", or "high" metrics.probe_accuracy float Overall probe accuracy metrics.n_shortcut_classes int Number of flagged classes metrics.n_classes int Total number of classes report.shortcut_classes list Class labels flagged as shortcuts report.class_rates dict Per-class TPR, FPR, and support report.top_dims_by_class dict Top-k important dimensions per class report.confusion_matrix list Confusion matrix from probe predictions

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Risk Level Condition Low No classes flagged as shortcuts Moderate Less than half of classes flagged High Half or more of classes flagged

docs.title: Example with Synthetic Data
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import FrequencyDetector
from shortcut_detect.datasets import generate_linear_shortcut

# Generate data with known shortcut
X, y = generate_linear_shortcut(
    n_samples=400,
    embedding_dim=24,
    shortcut_dims=4,
)

# Detect shortcut
detector = FrequencyDetector(
    top_percent=0.1,
    probe_evaluation="holdout",
    probe_holdout_frac=0.2,
)
detector.fit(X, y)

report = detector.get_report()
print(f"Shortcut detected: {report['shortcut_detected']}")
print(f"Risk level: {report['risk_level']}")
print(f"Shortcut classes: {report['report']['shortcut_classes']}")
print(f"Probe accuracy: {report['metrics']['probe_accuracy']:.2%}")

docs.title: Unified API Integration
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector

detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=["frequency"],
    seed=42,
    freq_top_percent=0.05,
    freq_tpr_threshold=0.5,
    freq_fpr_threshold=0.15,
    freq_probe_evaluation="holdout",
    freq_probe_holdout_frac=0.2,
)
detector.fit(embeddings, labels)
print(detector.summary())

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use Frequency Detector when:

  • You have only embeddings (no model access required)
  • You want to check if class signal concentrates in few dimensions
  • You need a fast, lightweight shortcut check
  • You want to identify which embedding dimensions carry class-separable shortcuts

Don't use Frequency Detector when:

  • You need to detect input-domain frequency artifacts (e.g., Fourier bands in images)
  • Your embeddings have very few dimensions (< 10)
  • You have very few samples (< 10)

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The detector is based on the observation that shortcut-reliant models tend to encode class information in a small subset of embedding dimensions. A logistic regression probe is trained to predict class labels from embeddings, and the resulting coefficient magnitudes indicate which dimensions carry the most class-separable information.

Per-class TPR and FPR:

$$\text{TPR}_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FN_c}, \quad \text{FPR}_c = \frac{FP_c}{FP_c + TN_c}$$

A class $c$ is flagged as a shortcut class when $\text{TPR}c \ge \tau}}$ and $\text{FPRc \le \tau$, indicating the probe can reliably identify and isolate this class from few dimensions.}

Top-k dimensions are extracted from the probe's coefficient matrix:

$$\text{top-k}_c = \text{argsort}(|w_c|)[-k:]$$

where $w_c$ is the coefficient vector for class $c$ and $k = \lceil \text{top_percent} \times d \rceil$.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Probe-based Detection - Complementary classifier approach
  • API Reference - Full API documentation
  • Overview - Compare all methods

docs.title: GCE (Generalized Cross Entropy) Detector
docs.text: Generalized Cross Entropy bias detector identifies minority or bias-conflicting samples by training a biased linear classifier with GCE loss. Samples that are hard for the biased classifier to fit (high per-sample loss) are flagged as potential shortcut-conflicting examples.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Train a linear classifier on embeddings with GCE loss (q ~ 0.7)
  2. Compute per-sample GCE loss on the training set
  3. Threshold losses at a configurable percentile (default: 90th)
  4. Flag high-loss samples as minority/bias-conflicting
  5. Assess risk based on the ratio of flagged samples
graph TD
    A[Embeddings + Labels] --> B[Train Linear Classifier with GCE Loss]
    B --> C[Compute Per-Sample GCE Losses]
    C --> D[Apply Percentile Threshold]
    D --> E{Loss >= Threshold?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Flag as Minority / Bias-Conflicting]
    E -->|No| G[Not Flagged]
    F --> H[Assess Risk Level]
    G --> H

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.gce import GCEDetector

detector = GCEDetector(
    q=0.7,
    loss_percentile_threshold=90.0,
    max_iter=500,
    random_state=42,
)

detector.fit(embeddings, labels)

# Inspect the report
report = detector.report_
print(f"Risk level: {report.risk_level}")
print(f"Minority ratio: {report.minority_ratio:.2%}")
print(f"Number of flagged samples: {report.n_minority}")

# Get indices of flagged samples
minority_idx = detector.get_minority_indices()

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description q float 0.7 GCE parameter in (0, 1]. Lower values downweight easy samples more aggressively loss_percentile_threshold float 90.0 Percentile (0-100) above which samples are flagged as minority max_iter int 500 Maximum L-BFGS-B iterations for the linear classifier random_state int 42 Random seed for reproducibility

docs.title: Report Structure (GCEDetectorReport)
docs.text: Field Type Description n_samples int Total number of samples n_minority int Number of flagged minority samples minority_ratio float Fraction of samples flagged loss_mean float Mean per-sample GCE loss loss_std float Standard deviation of per-sample GCE loss loss_min float Minimum per-sample GCE loss loss_max float Maximum per-sample GCE loss threshold float Loss threshold used for flagging q float GCE parameter used risk_level str "low", "moderate", or "high" notes str Human-readable risk summary

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Risk Level Condition Low Few high-loss samples flagged (minority ratio <= 10% and n_minority <= 20) Moderate Moderate flagged samples (minority ratio > 10% or n_minority > 20) High Many flagged samples (minority ratio > 25% or n_minority > 100)

docs.title: Example with Synthetic Data
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from shortcut_detect.gce import GCEDetector

# Create embeddings where a minority group differs
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 400
embeddings = rng.standard_normal((n, 16))
labels = np.array([0] * 200 + [1] * 200)

# Inject a shortcut: most class-1 samples share a spurious feature
embeddings[200:380, 0] += 3.0   # majority of class 1
embeddings[380:400, 0] -= 1.0   # minority subgroup of class 1

detector = GCEDetector(q=0.7, loss_percentile_threshold=90.0)
detector.fit(embeddings, labels)

print(f"Risk level: {detector.report_.risk_level}")
print(f"Minority samples: {detector.report_.n_minority}")
minority_idx = detector.get_minority_indices()
print(f"Flagged indices (first 10): {minority_idx[:10]}")

docs.title: Unified API Integration
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector

detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=["gce"],
    seed=42,
)
detector.fit(embeddings, labels)
print(detector.summary())

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use GCE Detector when:

  • You want to identify which samples are minority or bias-conflicting
  • You need a training-free (no GPU required) approach to flag hard samples
  • You want to understand the loss distribution across your dataset
  • You plan to use flagged samples for reweighting or resampling

Don't use GCE Detector when:

  • You have fewer than 2 distinct labels
  • Your dataset is very small (fewer than ~50 samples)
  • You need group-level fairness metrics (use Demographic Parity or Equalized Odds instead)

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The Generalized Cross Entropy loss is defined as:

$$L_i = \frac{1 - p_i^q}{q}$$

where $p_i$ is the predicted probability for the true class of sample $i$. When $q \to 0$, this recovers the standard cross-entropy loss. For $q \approx 0.7$, the loss downweights easy (high-confidence) samples and emphasizes hard ones.

A biased classifier trained with GCE loss tends to memorize majority patterns first. Samples with persistently high loss are those that conflict with the majority pattern: the minority or bias-conflicting examples that may indicate shortcut reliance.

docs.text:
• Demographic Parity - Group-level fairness detection
  • Equalized Odds - Another fairness-based approach

docs.title: Generative CVAE Counterfactual Detection
docs.text: The Generative CVAE detector trains a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) on embeddings conditioned on a binary spurious attribute. It generates counterfactual embeddings by encoding with the original attribute and decoding with the flipped attribute, then measures how a probe classifier's predictions change.

docs.title: What It Detects
docs.text:
• Whether a spurious (group) attribute causally influences model predictions in embedding space.
  • Large probe prediction shifts after counterfactual attribute flipping indicate shortcut reliance.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Train CVAE: A conditional VAE learns to reconstruct embeddings conditioned on the binary group label (spurious attribute).
  2. Train Attribute Predictor: A small linear network learns to predict the group label from embeddings.
  3. Generate Counterfactuals: For each sample, encode with the original group label and decode with the flipped label. Latent guidance optimizes the counterfactual to actually flip the predicted attribute while staying close to the original embedding.
  4. Evaluate Probe Shift: A probe classifier (internal LogisticRegression or user-provided) scores both original and counterfactual embeddings. Large prediction shifts indicate the model relies on the spurious attribute.

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text:
• embeddings: np.ndarray (n, d), representation space
  • group_labels: np.ndarray (n,), binary spurious attribute labels (0/1)

Optional:

  • labels: np.ndarray (n,), task labels (required for probe training; if omitted, detection is inconclusive)
  • probe_classifier: Pre-trained sklearn-like classifier or callable

docs.title: Unified API Example
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector

detector = ShortcutDetector(methods=["generative_cvae"])
detector.fit(embeddings=emb, labels=labels, group_labels=groups)

result = detector.get_results()["generative_cvae"]
print(result["metrics"])
print(result["shortcut_detected"])

docs.title: Direct API Example
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.causal import GenerativeCVEDetector

detector = GenerativeCVEDetector(epochs=50, random_state=42)
detector.fit(embeddings, group_labels, labels)

print(detector.results_["shortcut_detected"])
print(detector.results_["metrics"])
print(detector.summary())

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text: Metric Description mean_delta Mean probe prediction shift (original - counterfactual) frac_large_change Fraction of samples with mean_cosine_similarity Average cosine similarity between original and counterfactual embeddings probe_accuracy Accuracy of the internal/external probe

docs.title: Detection Rule
docs.text:
A shortcut is detected when both:

  • abs(mean_delta) > mean_delta_threshold (default: 1e-4)
  • frac_large_change > frac_large_threshold (default: 0.01)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• High risk: Large prediction shifts indicate the model relies heavily on the spurious attribute.
  • Low risk: Minimal prediction shifts suggest the spurious attribute has little influence.
  • Unknown: No probe available (labels not provided).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Parameter Default Description epochs 50 CVAE training epochs hidden 256 Hidden layer size zdim 64 Latent dimension guidance_steps 50 Latent optimization steps for counterfactual generation guidance_weight 5.0 Weight for attribute-flip loss proximity_weight 1.0 Weight for staying close to original embedding

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Requires binary group labels (0/1).
  • Detection thresholds are sensitive to dataset size and noise level.
  • CVAE quality depends on sufficient training data and appropriate hyperparameters.
  • Results can vary across random seeds, especially with small datasets.

docs.title: Geometric analysis
docs.text: Geometric analysis compares the groups' positions and shapes in embedding space: how far apart their centroids sit, and how much their principal subspaces overlap.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
For every pair of groups with at least min_group_size rows, GeometricShortcutAnalyzer:

  1. Computes centroids and the unit vector between them (the bias direction)
  2. Projects all embeddings onto that direction and measures the standardised gap between the two groups' mean projections (the effect size, a Cohen's d)
  3. Fits the top n_components principal directions of each group and measures the principal cosines between the two subspaces
  4. Flags a pair when its effect size is at or above effect_threshold, or its mean principal cosine is at or above subspace_cosine_threshold
graph TD
    A[Embeddings] --> B[Split by group]
    B --> C[Group centroids]
    C --> D[Bias direction and effect size]
    B --> E[Per-group principal directions]
    E --> F[Principal cosines between subspaces]
    D --> G[Risk level]
    F --> G

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import GeometricShortcutAnalyzer

analyzer = GeometricShortcutAnalyzer(n_components=5)
analyzer.fit(embeddings, group_labels)

print(analyzer.summary_)           # risk_level, message, num_high_effect_pairs, num_overlap_pairs
pair = analyzer.bias_pairs_[0]     # sorted by effect size, largest first
print(f"{pair.groups}: effect size {pair.effect_size:.2f}, gap {pair.projection_gap:.2f}")
sub = analyzer.subspace_pairs_[0]  # sorted by mean cosine, largest first
print(f"{sub.groups}: mean cosine {sub.mean_cosine:.2f}, smallest angle {sub.min_angle_deg:.1f} degrees")

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description n_components int 5 Principal directions kept per group min_group_size int 20 Groups with fewer rows are skipped effect_threshold float 0.8 Effect size at or above which a centroid pair counts as a signal subspace_cosine_threshold float 0.85 Mean principal cosine at or above which a subspace pair counts as a signal

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Type Description group_stats_ dict Per group, keyed by its label as a string: count, centroid, components (n_components by embedding_dim), variance_fraction, mask, projection_std bias_pairs_ list of BiasPairStats Per pair: groups, direction_norm, effect_size, projection_gap, alignment_score; sorted by effect size subspace_pairs_ list of SubspacePairStats Per pair: groups, mean_cosine, min_angle_deg, max_angle_deg; sorted by mean cosine summary_ dict risk_level, message, num_high_effect_pairs, num_overlap_pairs shortcut_detected_ bool True at moderate or high risk

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Risk Rule high at least one pair over the effect threshold and at least one over the cosine threshold moderate one of the two low neither

A large effect size means the groups sit apart along the line between their centroids. A high mean cosine means the groups' principal subspaces point the same way; the analyzer counts that as a second signal, on the reasoning that a shared dominant direction can carry the group. Both thresholds are fixed heuristics. The paper's audit calibrates a geometric statistic (centroid distance over within-group spread, within task strata) against a permutation null instead; see the Audit API.

docs.title: Bias direction analysis
docs.text:
The bias direction between two groups is the unit vector between their centroids. group_stats_ holds the centroids, so the direction and the projections are a few lines of NumPy:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

g0, g1 = analyzer.bias_pairs_[0].groups
c0, c1 = analyzer.group_stats_[g0]["centroid"], analyzer.group_stats_[g1]["centroid"]
direction = (c1 - c0) / np.linalg.norm(c1 - c0)
projections = embeddings @ direction

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
for group in (g0, g1):
    mask = analyzer.group_stats_[group]["mask"]
    ax.hist(projections[mask], bins=50, alpha=0.5, label=f"group {group}")
ax.set_xlabel("projection onto the bias direction")
ax.set_ylabel("count")
ax.legend()
plt.title(f"effect size {analyzer.bias_pairs_[0].effect_size:.2f}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("bias_direction.png")

docs.title: Subspace analysis
docs.text:
g0, g1 = analyzer.subspace_pairs_[0].groups
U0 = analyzer.group_stats_[g0]["components"]   # (n_components, embedding_dim)
U1 = analyzer.group_stats_[g1]["components"]
print(f"variance kept: {analyzer.group_stats_[g0]['variance_fraction']:.2f}, "
      f"{analyzer.group_stats_[g1]['variance_fraction']:.2f}")
print(f"mean principal cosine: {analyzer.subspace_pairs_[0].mean_cosine:.2f}")

The principal cosines are the singular values of $U_0 U_1^T$ after orthonormalising both bases; min_angle_deg and max_angle_deg are the matching angles.

docs.title: Several groups
docs.text:
fit accepts any number of groups; bias_pairs_ and subspace_pairs_ hold every pair:

for pair in analyzer.bias_pairs_:
    print(f"{pair.groups[0]} vs {pair.groups[1]}: effect size {pair.effect_size:.2f}")

docs.title: Removing the bias direction
docs.text:
Projecting the bias direction out of the embeddings is one step of linear debiasing. The analyzer has no method for it; with the direction computed above it is one line:

embeddings_debiased = embeddings - np.outer(embeddings @ direction, direction)

analyzer_after = GeometricShortcutAnalyzer()
analyzer_after.fit(embeddings_debiased, group_labels)
print(analyzer_after.summary_)
print(analyzer_after.bias_pairs_)   # [] when the two centroids now coincide

With two groups the projection makes the centroids coincide, so the analyzer drops that pair (bias_pairs_ is empty) and the risk level rests on the subspace test alone. The probe is the better check of what the projection removed; see Linear debiasing.

docs.title: Example with synthetic data
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import GeometricShortcutAnalyzer, generate_linear_shortcut

X, group = generate_linear_shortcut(n_samples=1000, embedding_dim=100, shortcut_dims=5, seed=42)

analyzer = GeometricShortcutAnalyzer(n_components=5)
analyzer.fit(X, group)
print(analyzer.summary_["risk_level"], f"{analyzer.bias_pairs_[0].effect_size:.2f}")

With five planted dimensions the centroid pair is far over the effect threshold, while the two groups' principal subspaces are not aligned, so the risk level is moderate (one signal of two).

docs.title: When to use geometric analysis
docs.text:
Use geometric analysis when:

  • You want to see the geometric structure of the bias
  • You plan to apply linear debiasing
  • You need an interpretable bias direction
  • Groups may occupy different subspaces

Don't use geometric analysis when:

  • Biases are highly non-linear
  • You have very few samples per group (< 30)
  • Embeddings are very high-dimensional relative to samples

docs.title: Bias direction
docs.text:
$$\mathbf{d} = \frac{\mu_1 - \mu_0}{||\mu_1 - \mu_0||}$$

where $\mu_g$ is the centroid of group $g$.

docs.title: Effect size
docs.text:
Cohen's d along the bias direction:

$$d = \frac{|\bar{p}_1 - \bar{p}0|}{s$$}}

where $\bar{p}g$ is the mean projection of group $g$ onto the bias direction and $s$ the pooled standard deviation of the projections.}

docs.title: Subspace overlap
docs.text:
With $U_0$ and $U_1$ the orthonormalised principal bases of the two groups, the principal cosines are the singular values $\sigma_i$ of $U_0^T U_1$ and the overlap score is their mean:

$$\text{overlap} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i$$

A pair counts as a signal when this mean is at or above subspace_cosine_threshold.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• HBAC clustering: clustering-based detection
  • API reference: full API documentation
  • Overview: compare all methods

docs.title: GradCAM Analysis
docs.text: GradCAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) visualizes which input regions your model focuses on when making predictions. When combined with shortcut detection, it reveals whether the model attends to spurious features correlated with protected attributes.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Generate heatmaps for each input showing model attention
  2. Compare attention patterns between protected groups
  3. Measure overlap between attention and known shortcut regions
  4. Identify if the model focuses on different features for different groups
graph TD
    A[Input Image] --> B[Forward Pass]
    B --> C[Target Layer Activations]
    B --> D[Gradients]
    C --> E[Weighted Activations]
    D --> E
    E --> F[GradCAM Heatmap]
    F --> G[Compare Across Groups]
    G --> H[Shortcut Attention Analysis]

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import GradCAMHeatmapGenerator
import torch

# Load your model
model = torch.load("model.pth")
model.eval()

# Specify target layer (usually last conv layer)
target_layer = model.features[-1]  # Adjust for your architecture

# Create GradCAM generator
gradcam = GradCAMHeatmapGenerator(
    model=model,
    target_layer=target_layer,
    device='cuda'
)

# Generate heatmap for an image
heatmap = gradcam.generate(image_tensor, target_class=1)

# Visualize
gradcam.visualize(image_tensor, heatmap, save_path="attention.png")

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description model nn.Module required PyTorch model target_layer nn.Module required Layer to compute GradCAM on device str 'cuda' Device for computation use_guided bool False Use Guided GradCAM

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Returns Description generate(input, class) ndarray Heatmap for given input and class generate_batch(inputs, classes) list[ndarray] Batch heatmap generation visualize(input, heatmap) None Overlay heatmap on input compare_groups(inputs, groups) AttentionOverlapResult Compare attention across groups

docs.title: AttentionOverlapResult
docs.text:
@dataclass
class AttentionOverlapResult:
    overlap_score: float        # Attention overlap between groups
    group_heatmaps: dict        # Average heatmap per group
    divergence_regions: ndarray # Regions with divergent attention
    summary: str                # Human-readable summary

docs.title: Attention Comparison
docs.text:
Compare model attention between protected groups:

from shortcut_detect import GradCAMHeatmapGenerator

# Generate heatmaps for all samples
heatmaps = []
for image in images:
    heatmap = gradcam.generate(image, target_class=predictions[i])
    heatmaps.append(heatmap)
heatmaps = np.stack(heatmaps)

# Compare attention between groups
result = gradcam.compare_groups(heatmaps, group_labels)

print(f"Attention overlap: {result.overlap_score:.2f}")
print(result.summary)

# Visualize divergent regions
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

axes[0].imshow(result.group_heatmaps[0], cmap='jet')
axes[0].set_title('Group 0 Average Attention')

axes[1].imshow(result.group_heatmaps[1], cmap='jet')
axes[1].set_title('Group 1 Average Attention')

axes[2].imshow(result.divergence_regions, cmap='RdBu')
axes[2].set_title('Attention Divergence')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('attention_comparison.png')

docs.title: Shortcut Detection with GradCAM
docs.text:
Detect if the model attends to shortcut features:

# Define shortcut region (e.g., hospital watermark location)
shortcut_mask = np.zeros((224, 224))
shortcut_mask[10:50, 10:100] = 1  # Top-left corner

# Measure attention overlap with shortcut region
def shortcut_attention(heatmap, shortcut_mask):
    """Fraction of attention on shortcut region."""
    heatmap_norm = heatmap / heatmap.sum()
    return (heatmap_norm * shortcut_mask).sum()

# Check each sample
shortcut_attention_scores = []
for heatmap in heatmaps:
    score = shortcut_attention(heatmap, shortcut_mask)
    shortcut_attention_scores.append(score)

print(f"Mean attention on shortcut: {np.mean(shortcut_attention_scores):.2%}")
print(f"Samples with >10% shortcut attention: {(np.array(shortcut_attention_scores) > 0.1).mean():.2%}")

docs.title: Layer Selection
docs.text:
Choose the right layer for GradCAM:

# For ResNet
target_layer = model.layer4[-1]  # Last residual block

# For VGG
target_layer = model.features[-1]  # Last conv layer

# For Vision Transformers (ViT)
target_layer = model.blocks[-1].norm1  # Last attention block

# For custom models, find conv layers
def find_conv_layers(model):
    conv_layers = []
    for name, module in model.named_modules():
        if isinstance(module, torch.nn.Conv2d):
            conv_layers.append((name, module))
    return conv_layers

layers = find_conv_layers(model)
print("Available conv layers:", [name for name, _ in layers])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

# Original image
axes[0].imshow(image_tensor.permute(1, 2, 0).cpu())
axes[0].set_title('Original')
axes[0].axis('off')

# Heatmap

docs.text:
For sharper visualizations:

gradcam = GradCAMHeatmapGenerator(
    model=model,
    target_layer=target_layer,
    use_guided=True  # Enable Guided GradCAM

# Generates sharper, more localized heatmaps
heatmap_guided = gradcam.generate(image_tensor, target_class=1)

docs.title: Batch Processing
docs.text:
Efficient processing of many images:

from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

# Create dataloader
dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=False)

# Process batches
all_heatmaps = []
for batch in dataloader:
    images, labels, groups = batch
    images = images.to('cuda')

    heatmaps = gradcam.generate_batch(images, labels)
    all_heatmaps.extend(heatmaps)

# Analyze by group
all_heatmaps = np.stack(all_heatmaps)
result = gradcam.compare_groups(all_heatmaps, all_groups)

docs.title: When to Use GradCAM
docs.text:
Use GradCAM when:

  • You have access to the model architecture
  • You want visual explanations of shortcuts
  • You're working with image data
  • You need to identify specific image regions causing bias

Don't use GradCAM when:

  • You only have embeddings (no model access)
  • Working with non-image data
  • GPU is unavailable (very slow on CPU)
  • Model uses attention mechanisms (consider attention visualization instead)

docs.title: Integration with ShortcutDetector
docs.text:
GradCAM works alongside other detection methods:

from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector, GradCAMHeatmapGenerator

# First, detect shortcuts with embedding-based methods
detector = ShortcutDetector(methods=['hbac', 'probe', 'statistical'])
detector.fit(embeddings, group_labels)

# Check if probe accuracy indicates shortcuts
results = detector.get_results()
if results['probe']['accuracy'] > 0.7:
    print("Shortcuts detected! Using GradCAM for visual analysis...")

    # Then use GradCAM to visualize where shortcuts manifest
    gradcam = GradCAMHeatmapGenerator(model, target_layer)
    result = gradcam.compare_groups(images, group_labels)

    print(f"Attention overlap: {result.overlap_score:.2f}")
    print("Saving divergence visualization...")
    plt.imsave('divergence.png', result.divergence_regions, cmap='RdBu')

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
GradCAM computes importance weights by global-average-pooling gradients:

$$\alpha_k^c = \frac{1}{Z} \sum_i \sum_j \frac{\partial y^c}{\partial A_{ij}^k}$$

The heatmap is a weighted combination of feature maps:

$$L_{\text{GradCAM}}^c = \text{ReLU}\left(\sum_k \alpha_k^c A^k\right)$$

Where:

  • $y^c$ is the score for class $c$
  • $A^k$ is the $k$-th feature map
  • $Z$ is the spatial size of feature maps

docs.title: GroupDRO (Worst-Group Robustness)
docs.text:
Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (GroupDRO) detects shortcuts by measuring performance disparities across predefined groups. If a model performs significantly worse on one group than others, it is strong evidence that the embeddings encode group-dependent shortcuts or biases.

Unlike clustering-based methods, GroupDRO is supervised and optimization-based: it trains a classifier on embeddings while adversarially emphasizing the worst-performing group.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
GroupDRO trains a lightweight classifier on embeddings using a robust objective that minimizes the worst-group loss instead of the average loss.

At each training step:

  1. Compute per-group losses for the current batch
  2. Update adversarial group weights to emphasize high-loss groups
  3. Optimize the classifier using the weighted (robust) loss
  4. Track worst-group vs average performance
graph TD
    A[Embeddings + Labels + Groups] --> B[Classifier]
    B --> C[Per-group Losses]
    C --> D[Update Adversarial Weights q]
    D --> E[Robust Loss = q · group_loss]
    E --> B

If one group consistently receives high adversarial weight and low accuracy, this indicates shortcut reliance or group-specific failure modes.

docs.title: Via the Unified API (Recommended)
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector
import numpy as np

# Precomputed embeddings
embeddings = np.load("embeddings.npy")
labels = np.load("labels.npy")
group_labels = np.load("groups.npy")  # required

detector = ShortcutDetector(methods=["groupdro"])
detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels=group_labels)

print(detector.summary())
detector.generate_report("groupdro_report.html")

docs.title: Standalone Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.groupdro import GroupDRODetector, GroupDROConfig

config = GroupDROConfig(
    n_epochs=10,
    alpha=0.2,
    robust_step_size=0.01,
)

detector = GroupDRODetector(config)
detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels)

report = detector.get_report()["report"]
print(report["final"]["worst_group_acc"])

docs.title: Advanced: Loader Hooks for GroupDRO
docs.text:
You can customize DataLoader creation while keeping GroupDRO training logic unchanged.

import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

def groupdro_loader_factory(req):
    # req.stage in {"train", "val", "full"} depending on path
    return DataLoader(
        req.dataset,
        batch_size=req.batch_size,
        shuffle=req.shuffle,
        num_workers=req.num_workers,
        pin_memory=req.pin_memory,
        drop_last=req.drop_last,
        **req.extra_kwargs,
    )

config = GroupDROConfig(
    n_epochs=5,
    loader_factory=groupdro_loader_factory,
    stage_loader_overrides={"train": {"batch_size": 256}},
)

docs.title: Advanced: File-Backed Datasets (Large Data)
docs.text:
GroupDRODetector now supports loader-native training via fit_dataset(...) and fit_loaders(...).

import torch
from shortcut_detect.groupdro.groupdro import GroupDROConfig, GroupDRODetector

class GroupDataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __init__(self, rows):
        self.rows = rows

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.rows)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        x = load_embedding_from_file(self.rows[idx])  # shape (d,)
        y = load_label(self.rows[idx])                # class id
        g = load_group(self.rows[idx])                # protected group id
        return {"embeddings": x, "labels": y, "group_labels": g}

cfg = GroupDROConfig(n_epochs=5, batch_size=128, device="cpu")
detector = GroupDRODetector(cfg)
detector.fit_dataset(GroupDataset(index_rows))

For IterableDataset inputs, pass a validation dataset and data_spec:

detector.fit_dataset(
    train_iterable,
    val_dataset=val_iterable,
    data_spec={"n_features": 512, "n_classes": 2, "n_groups": 3},
)

docs.title: Example with Synthetic Data
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector
import numpy as np

# Synthetic dataset with a hard group
X, y, g = generate_linear_shortcut(
    n_samples=800,

g[:400] = 0

  • Worst-group accuracy significantly lower than average
  • Adversarial weights concentrate on the harder group

docs.title: When to Use GroupDRO
docs.text:
Use GroupDRO when:

  • You have explicit group labels (e.g. demographics, environments)
  • You want quantitative evidence of group disparities
  • You suspect shortcuts tied to protected attributes
  • You want training-time signals, not just geometry

Don’t use GroupDRO when:

  • Group labels are unavailable
  • You want fully unsupervised detection (use HBAC)
  • Dataset is extremely small (< 100 samples)
  • Groups are perfectly balanced and indistinguishable

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
GroupDRO solves:

$$ \min_\theta \max_{q \in \Delta} \sum_{g=1}^G q_g , \mathcal{L}_g(\theta) $$

Where:

  • $\mathcal{L}_g$ is the loss on group $g$
  • $q$ is an adversarial distribution over groups
  • $\Delta$ is the probability simplex

The adversarial update is:

$$ q_g \leftarrow \frac{q_g \exp(\eta \cdot \ell_g)}{\sum_{h} q_h \exp(\eta \cdot \ell_h)} $$

This forces the model to focus on its worst-performing groups, making GroupDRO an effective bias detector when performance gaps persist.
