docs.title: HBAC clustering
docs.text: Hierarchical Bias-Aware Clustering checks whether the embeddings split into clusters that are nearly pure in the group label, and whether a linear classifier separates the groups. Both are signs that the group is easy to read off the embedding.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
HBACDetector (an alias of EmbeddingShortcutDetector) standardises the embeddings, holds out test_size of the rows, and then:

  1. Splits the training rows with 2-means, up to max_iterations times, each time splitting the cluster whose labels vary most; sub-clusters smaller than min_cluster_size of the training rows are dropped
  2. Scores purity per cluster: the share of its rows that carry the dominant label
  3. Ranks dimensions with a one-way ANOVA of each dimension against the label
  4. Tests linearity with a logistic regression fitted on the training rows and scored on the held-out rows
  5. Decides: shortcut if two or more clusters have purity above 0.8, or if fewer than 10% of the dimensions are significant (p < 0.01) and the held-out linear accuracy is above 0.85
graph TD
    A[Embeddings] --> B[Standardise, hold out test rows]
    B --> C[2-means split of the most mixed cluster]
    C --> D{max_iterations reached?}
    D -->|No| C
    D -->|Yes| E[Cluster purities]
    B --> F[ANOVA per dimension]
    B --> G[Logistic regression, held-out accuracy]
    E --> H[Decision]
    F --> H
    G --> H

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import HBACDetector

detector = HBACDetector(
    max_iterations=3,       # number of 2-means splits
    min_cluster_size=0.05,  # smallest cluster kept, as a fraction of the training rows
    random_state=42,
)
detector.fit(embeddings, group_labels)

verdict = detector.shortcut_report_["has_shortcut"]
print(f"Shortcut detected: {detector.shortcut_detected_} ({verdict['confidence']} confidence)")
print(f"Signals: {verdict['types']}")
print(f"Linear test accuracy: {detector.shortcut_report_['linearity_score']['test_accuracy']:.2f}")
for cluster in detector.shortcut_report_["cluster_purities"]:
    print(f"cluster {cluster['cluster_id']}: {cluster['size']} rows, purity {cluster['purity']:.2f}")

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description max_iterations int 3 Number of 2-means splits min_cluster_size float 0.01 Smallest cluster kept, as a fraction of the training rows test_size float 0.2 Share of rows held out for the linearity test random_state int 42 Seed for the split and for k-means config HBACConfig None Frozen dataclass with the same four fields; takes precedence when given

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: Attribute Type Description shortcut_detected_ bool Whether the decision rule fired shortcut_report_ dict cluster_purities (one dict per cluster: cluster_id, size, purity, dominant_label), dimension_importance (DataFrame with a p_value per dimension), linearity_score (train_accuracy, test_accuracy, overfitting), statistical_tests, has_shortcut (exists, confidence, types, evidence) clusters_ list One dict per final cluster with its training row indices and labels results_ dict The standard detector schema; get_report() returns it, summary() prints one line and get_report_text() a longer text

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Signal Shortcut evidence Purity two or more clusters above 0.8 Linearity held-out accuracy above 0.85, together with few significant dimensions

confidence is high when two signals fire, medium with one and low with none. These thresholds are fixed heuristics. The paper's audit uses an HBAC statistic (normalised mutual information between k-means clusters and the attribute, within task strata) calibrated against a permutation null instead; see the Audit API.

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
visualize projects the embeddings to two dimensions and colours them by cluster and by label:

detector.visualize(method="pca", save_path="hbac_pca.png")   # or method="tsne"

docs.title: Example with synthetic data
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import HBACDetector, generate_linear_shortcut

# 500 embeddings of width 100; the first 5 dimensions separate the two groups
X, group = generate_linear_shortcut(n_samples=500, embedding_dim=100, shortcut_dims=5, seed=42)

detector = HBACDetector(random_state=42)
detector.fit(X, group)

verdict = detector.shortcut_report_["has_shortcut"]
print(detector.shortcut_detected_, verdict["confidence"], verdict["types"])
print(detector.summary())

On this data the held-out linear accuracy is 1.0 and the clusters are pure, so the detector flags a shortcut with high confidence.

docs.title: When to use HBAC
docs.text:
Use HBAC when:

  • You want to see whether the groups form separate clusters
  • Your embeddings may have natural cluster boundaries
  • You need a fast check (two k-means splits and one logistic regression)

Don't use HBAC when:

  • Groups are uniformly mixed (no clusters)
  • You have very few samples (< 50)
  • Groups have highly overlapping distributions

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
HBAC rests on the observation that if a model has learned a shortcut, embeddings from the same group will be more similar to each other than to embeddings from other groups.

Purity of cluster $c_k$ is the share of its rows carrying the dominant group:

$$\text{Purity}(c_k) = \frac{1}{|c_k|} \max_j |c_k \cap g_j|$$

where $g_j$ is group $j$.

Linearity is the held-out accuracy of a logistic regression predicting the group from the standardised embedding.

docs.title: Intersectional Fairness Analysis
docs.text:
Intersectional detects shortcuts by evaluating fairness metrics across intersections of demographic attributes (e.g., Black + Female, White + Male).

Based on Buolamwini & Gebru (2018, Gender Shades), single-attribute fairness analysis can miss compounded disparities at intersections. For example, Black women may have worse model accuracy than all other groups, even when race-only or gender-only analysis shows smaller gaps.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The Intersectional detector:

  1. Combines demographic attributes from extra_labels (e.g., race and gender) into intersection groups (e.g., "Black_Female", "White_Male")
  2. Filters samples with missing values and groups below min_group_size
  3. Runs Equalized Odds and Demographic Parity on the intersection groups
  4. Produces TPR/FPR/positive-rate metrics per intersection and aggregated gaps
graph TD
    A[Embeddings + Labels + extra_labels] --> B[Build Intersection Groups]
    B --> C[Filter Small Groups]
    C --> D[Equalized Odds on Intersections]
    C --> E[Demographic Parity on Intersections]
    D --> F[Merge Report]
    E --> F
    F --> G[IntersectionalReport]

Key insight: Disparities can compound at intersections. A model may appear fair on race alone or gender alone, yet show large gaps for specific intersections like Black women.

docs.title: Via the Unified API (Recommended)
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector
import numpy as np

# Precomputed embeddings
embeddings = np.load("embeddings.npy")
labels = np.load("labels.npy")  # Binary labels required

# At least 2 demographic attributes required
extra_labels = {
    "race": np.array(["Black", "White", "Asian", ...]),
    "gender": np.array(["Male", "Female", "Male", ...]),
}

detector = ShortcutDetector(methods=["intersectional"])
detector.fit(embeddings, labels, extra_labels=extra_labels)

print(detector.summary())

docs.title: Standalone Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.fairness import IntersectionalDetector

detector = IntersectionalDetector(
    min_group_size=10,
    tpr_gap_threshold=0.1,
    fpr_gap_threshold=0.1,
    dp_gap_threshold=0.1,
)

detector.fit(embeddings, labels, extra_labels)

print(f"TPR Gap: {detector.tpr_gap_:.3f}")
print(f"FPR Gap: {detector.fpr_gap_:.3f}")
print(f"DP Gap: {detector.dp_gap_:.3f}")
print(f"Risk Level: {detector.report_.risk_level}")

docs.text:
• extra_labels: Dictionary with at least 2 demographic attribute arrays (e.g., {"race": ..., "gender": ...}). Values can be strings or categorical codes.
  • Reserved keys spurious and early_epoch_reps are excluded from intersection attributes.
  • Binary labels required for the task (same as Equalized Odds).

docs.title: Custom CSV Format
docs.text:
For the dashboard or custom CSV upload:

  • Embeddings mode: Include attr_race and attr_gender columns (or group_label + attr_gender) for intersectional analysis.
  • Sample data: CheXpert demo uses PRIMARY_RACE and GENDER from the demographics file.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• You want intersectional fairness beyond single-attribute analysis
  • You have multiple demographic attributes (e.g., race, gender)
  • You want to detect compounded disparities at intersections (e.g., Buolamwini & Gebru 2018)
  • You need regulatory or fairness reporting across subgroups

docs.title: Last Layer Retraining (M06 DFR)
docs.text: Last Layer Retraining (DFR, Deep Feature Reweighting) is a model-level mitigation (Kirichenko et al. 2023) that retrains only the last linear layer on a group-balanced subset of embeddings. The embeddings stay frozen; only the classifier is retrained. This simple approach can match or outperform more complex debiasing methods.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Kirichenko, P., Izmailov, P., & Wilson, A. G. (2023). Last Layer Re-Training is Sufficient for Robustness to Spurious Correlations. ICLR 2023. arXiv:2204.02937

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
• Input: Embeddings, task labels (target to predict), and group/protected labels.
  • Training: Build a group-balanced subset (equal samples per group), then fit a LogisticRegression classifier on this subset. StandardScaler preprocesses embeddings. The class balances over whatever group_labels it is given; the paper's protocol, and the dashboard, pass attribute x task label groups (2 * A + Y), so the subset is balanced over the attribute x label cells (four when A is binary) and holds the smallest cell's size times the number of cells.
  • In the paper: at the package defaults (L1 penalty, C=1, balanced class weights) DFR was the only mitigation that lowered the confounded head's TPR gap on CheXpert, from 0.18 to 0.01 on average, while task AUROC fell from 0.73 to 0.65. The embedding is unchanged, so the audit score is unchanged by construction.
  • Output: Trained classifier that predicts task labels. Output CSV includes original data plus dfr_prediction column.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• scikit-learn (already a dependency of shortkit-ml).
  • NumPy.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import LastLayerRetraining
import numpy as np

# Embeddings (n_samples, embed_dim), task labels, and group labels
embeddings = ...  # shape (N, D)
task_labels = ...  # shape (N,), e.g., class 0/1
group_labels = ...  # shape (N,), e.g., demographic group 0/1/2

dfr = LastLayerRetraining(
    C=1.0,
    penalty="l1",
    class_weight="balanced",
    random_state=42,
)
dfr.fit(embeddings, task_labels, group_labels)
predictions = dfr.predict(embeddings)

docs.title: Convenience: fit_predict
docs.text: predictions = dfr.fit_predict(embeddings, task_labels, group_labels)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• C: Inverse regularization strength (default 1.0). Smaller = stronger regularization.
  • penalty: "l1" or "l2" (default "l1").
  • solver: Solver for LogisticRegression (default "liblinear").
  • class_weight: "balanced" or None for imbalanced task labels (default "balanced").
  • random_state: Seed for reproducibility.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Run detection and export embeddings with task_label and group_label.
  2. Fit LastLayerRetraining on embeddings, task labels, and group labels.
  3. Use predict() to obtain task predictions for new or existing embeddings.
  4. Compare worst-group accuracy before vs. after DFR.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Spurious correlation between group and task (e.g., Waterbirds, CelebA).
  • You have embeddings and group labels but cannot retrain the full model.
  • You want a simple, fast mitigation (sklearn only) vs. adversarial training (M04).

docs.title: Detection methods overview
docs.text: ShortKit-ML provides several complementary methods for detecting shortcuts in embedding spaces; 19 are registered as ShortcutDetector keys. Each method has different strengths and is sensitive to different types of biases.

docs.title: Why several methods?
docs.text: Each method reads a different property of the embedding (cluster structure, per-dimension differences, centroid distance, a fitted direction), and the secondary scores are on interpretable scales. Agreement between methods is reported as a description. It is not a decision rule: in the paper's synthetic benchmark the detectors' flags were strongly correlated, and requiring several to agree lowered sensitivity without a useful gain in specificity.

docs.title: The paper's audit
docs.text: The accompanying paper runs shortcut_detect.audit.conditional_audit. The risk levels on these pages play no part in it. Its single primary test is the conditional probe: an L2 logistic regression predicting the attribute from the embedding concatenated with the task label, scored by out-of-fold AUROC (5-fold CV stratified on attribute and task, grouped by patient when groups is given). The null is a conditional permutation: the attribute is shuffled within task-label strata, between patients where patient ids exist, K times; the p-value is (1 + number of null statistics at or above the observed) / (K + 1). The five secondary detectors (statistical, geometric, bias direction PCA, HBAC, frequency) share that null, and the six p-values of a cell are Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted. The number of flagged detectors is reported as a description only. AuditConfig defaults: C=1.0, n_clusters=8, top_k_fraction=0.05, n_permutations=200; the clinical audits set n_permutations_probe=500. SIS, the fairness gaps and the training-dynamics methods are outside the score. The audit measures shortcut potential, whether the attribute is recoverable from the embedding given the task; a positive result does not show that a classifier trained on the embedding uses the attribute. Reference: Audit API.

optional interventional data VAE Disentangled latent shortcut dimensions Discovers latent factors; human-interpretable traversals Requires raw images; VAE training cost Frequency Concentrated class-separable dimensions Embedding-only, no model access needed Assumes linear probe sufficiency Generative CVAE Spurious attribute influence via counterfactuals Generates embedding-space counterfactuals; measures causal effect Requires binary group labels; seed-sensitive Shortcut Masking (M01) Mitigation: mask/inpaint shortcut regions Data augmentation for retraining (Teso & Kersting 2019) Requires shortcut regions/dims from detection Background Randomization (M02) Mitigation: swap foregrounds with random backgrounds Reduces background shortcuts (Kwon et al. 2023) Requires foreground masks; needs at least 2 images Adversarial Debiasing (M04) Mitigation: remove demographic encoding Adversarial training (Zhang et al. 2018) Requires protected labels; PyTorch Explanation Regularization (M05) Mitigation: penalize gradients on shortcut regions RRR (Ross et al. 2017) Requires model, images, labels, shortcut masks; docs.title: For production audits
docs.text:
Use the paper's audit (conditional_audit) for the measurement. To explore alongside it, run several methods:

detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=['hbac', 'probe', 'statistical', 'geometric', 'equalized_odds', 'demographic_parity', 'intersectional', 'groupdro']
)

docs.title: For quick screening
docs.text:
Use fast methods for initial assessment:

detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=['statistical', 'probe']
)

docs.title: For deep analysis
docs.text:
Use all methods plus GradCAM for visual insights:

detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=['hbac', 'probe', 'statistical', 'geometric']
)
# Plus GradCAM separately for visual analysis
gradcam = GradCAMHeatmapGenerator(model, target_layer)

docs.title: Risk assessment
docs.text:
Each method applies a fixed rule to decide whether it flags a shortcut (the defaults, from the code):

Method Flagged when HBAC two or more clusters have purity above 0.8, or few dimensions matter and the held-out linear accuracy is above 0.85 Probe the held-out metric (f1 by default) exceeds threshold=0.70; risk high from 0.85 Statistical any dimension stays significant after the multiple-testing correction (fdr_bh, alpha 0.05) Geometric a centroid pair has effect size at or above 0.8, or a subspace pair has mean cosine at or above 0.85 Equalized odds the TPR or FPR gap between groups is at or above 0.1 Demographic parity the positive-rate gap between groups is at or above 0.1 GroupDRO average accuracy minus worst-group accuracy exceeds 0.10

These rules are heuristics for exploration. The paper's audit calibrates each statistic against a permutation null instead and reads nothing off these thresholds.

docs.title: Aggregated risk
docs.text:
The unified ShortcutDetector provides an aggregated assessment via the summary() method. The aggregation strategy is controlled by the condition_name parameter:

Condition Strategy Best For indicator_count (default) Counts total risk indicators. 2+ = HIGH, 1 = MODERATE, 0 = LOW Simple audits, general use majority_vote Counts methods with indicators as votes Conservative consensus-based screening weighted_risk Weights each detector by evidence strength (probe accuracy, stat significance, HBAC confidence, geometric effect size) Graded scoring multi_attribute Cross-references risk across sensitive attributes; escalates when multiple attributes flag risk Multi-demographic analysis (race + sex + age) meta_classifier Trained sklearn meta-classifier on detector features, or heuristic fallback Advanced pipelines with synthetic training data 
# Default aggregation
detector = ShortcutDetector(methods=['hbac', 'probe', 'statistical'])
detector.fit(embeddings, labels)
print(detector.summary())

# Weighted risk for nuanced scoring
detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=['hbac', 'probe', 'statistical', 'geometric'],
    condition_name='weighted_risk',
)
detector.fit(embeddings, labels)
print(detector.summary())

# Access individual method results
results = detector.get_results()
print(results['probe']['results']['metrics']['metric_value'])   # probe score (f1 by default)
print(results['hbac']['report']['has_shortcut']['exists'])      # HBAC decision
print(results['probe']['risk_value'], results['hbac']['risk_value'])

docs.title: Detailed method guides
docs.text:
Learn more about each method:

  • HBAC Clustering - Hierarchical clustering analysis
  • Probe-based Detection - Classifier-based information leakage
  • Statistical Testing - Feature-wise hypothesis tests
  • Geometric Analysis - Subspace and direction analysis
  • Equalized Odds - TPR/FPR fairness analysis
  • Intersectional Analysis - Fairness across demographic intersections
  • SIS (Sufficient Input Subsets) - Minimal embedding dimensions for prediction (Carter et al. 2019)
  • Early-Epoch Clustering - Early training shortcut clustering
  • GroupDRO - Worst-group robustness analysis
  • GradCAM - Visual attention analysis
  • SpRAy - Heatmap clustering for Clever Hans detection
  • CAV - Concept activation vector testing
  • Causal Effect - Causal effect regularization for spurious attribute detection
  • VAE - VAE-based shortcut detection via latent disentanglement
  • Frequency - Embedding-space frequency shortcut detection
  • Generative CVAE - Conditional VAE counterfactual shortcut detection
  • Shortcut Masking (M01) - Data mitigation: mask/inpaint shortcut regions
  • Background Randomization (M02) - Data mitigation: swap foregrounds with random backgrounds
  • Adversarial Debiasing (M04) - Model mitigation: adversarial training to remove demographic encoding
  • Explanation Regularization (M05) - Model mitigation: penalize input gradients on shortcut regions
  • Last Layer Retraining (M06) - Model mitigation: retrain last layer on group-balanced subset
  • Contrastive Debiasing (M07) - Model mitigation: contrastive learning to separate shortcuts

docs.title: Method limitations
docs.text:
All methods have limitations you should be aware of:

  1. Sample Size - Most methods need sufficient samples per group (n > 30)
  2. Linearity - Some methods assume linear relationships
  3. Independence - Assumes embeddings are i.i.d. samples; when several images come from one patient, pass patient ids as groups to conditional_audit so folds and permutations are patient-level
  4. Single Protected Attribute - Most fairness methods assume one protected attribute; use Intersectional Analysis for multiple attributes.

docs.title: Probe-based detection
docs.text:
Probe-based detection tests whether the group can be predicted from the embedding. If a classifier trained on the embeddings predicts group membership well, the embeddings carry group information.

The paper's conditional probe

The thresholds on this page belong to the interactive SKLearnProbe and decide nothing in the paper. The paper's primary test is the conditional probe in shortcut_detect.audit.conditional_audit: an L2 logistic regression (C=1.0) predicts the attribute from the standardised embedding concatenated with the task label; the score is the out-of-fold AUROC of 5-fold cross-validation stratified on attribute and task and grouped by patient; the p-value comes from permuting the attribute within task-label strata, between patients where patient ids are given (K=500 in the clinical audits). Conditioning on the task label is what keeps an embedding that encodes only the task from being flagged when attribute and task are correlated.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Train a classifier on the embeddings to predict the group
  2. Score it on held-out rows (or by cross-validation)
  3. Flag a shortcut when the score exceeds a threshold
graph LR
    A[Embeddings] --> B[Probe classifier]
    B --> C[Predicted group]
    C --> D[Compare to true group]
    D --> E[Held-out score]
    E --> F{Above threshold?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Shortcut detected]
    F -->|No| H[No shortcut]

docs.title: SKLearnProbe
docs.text:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from shortcut_detect import SKLearnProbe

probe = SKLearnProbe(
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
    metric="accuracy",      # or "f1" (default), "precision", "recall", "roc_auc"
    evaluation="holdout",   # or "cv", "train"
    test_size=0.2,
    threshold=0.70,
    random_state=42,
)
probe.fit(embeddings, group_labels)   # the probe splits the data itself

print(f"held-out accuracy: {probe.metric_value_:.2%}")
print(f"flagged: {probe.shortcut_detected_} (risk {probe.get_report()['risk_level']})")

fit takes the whole dataset and does the split or the cross-validation internally. With estimator=None the probe is a standardised logistic regression. The risk level is high when the metric reaches max(threshold, 0.85), moderate when it reaches threshold, and low below.

docs.title: TorchProbe
docs.text:
For GPU training or a custom architecture:

import torch.nn as nn
from shortcut_detect import TorchProbe

class MLPProbe(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, n_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, 256),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.3),
            nn.Linear(256, n_classes),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.layers(x)

probe = TorchProbe(
    model=MLPProbe(512, 3),        # 512-dim embeddings, 3 groups
    loss_fn=nn.CrossEntropyLoss(),
    device="cuda",                 # None picks cuda when available, else cpu
    epochs=50,
    optimizer_kwargs={"lr": 1e-3},
)
probe.fit(embeddings, group_labels)
print(probe.metric_value_, probe.shortcut_detected_)

docs.title: Advanced: externalize the DataLoader
docs.text:
TorchProbe builds its own loaders by default; a loader factory and per-stage overrides replace them:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

def probe_loader_factory(req):
    # req.stage in {"train", "val", "eval", "predict"}
    return DataLoader(
        req.dataset,
        batch_size=req.batch_size,
        shuffle=req.shuffle,
        num_workers=req.num_workers,
        pin_memory=req.pin_memory,
        drop_last=req.drop_last,
        **req.extra_kwargs,
    )

probe = TorchProbe(
    model=MLPProbe(512, 3),
    loss_fn=nn.CrossEntropyLoss(),
    loader_factory=probe_loader_factory,
    stage_loader_overrides={"predict": {"batch_size": 16}},
)

docs.title: Advanced: file-backed datasets
docs.text:
fit_dataset(...) trains from a map-style or iterable dataset without loading everything into RAM:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from shortcut_detect.probes import TorchProbe

class EmbeddingDataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __init__(self, rows):
        self.rows = rows  # file index / metadata

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.rows)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        x = load_embedding_from_file(self.rows[idx])   # shape (d,)
        y = load_group_label(self.rows[idx])           # int class id
        return {"embeddings": x, "labels": y}

probe = TorchProbe(
    model=nn.Linear(512, 2),
    loss_fn=nn.CrossEntropyLoss(),
    metric="accuracy",
    device="cpu",
)
probe.fit_dataset(EmbeddingDataset(index_rows))

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Attribute Type Description metric_value_ float The held-out (or cross-validated) score shortcut_detected_ bool metric_value_ > threshold estimator_ estimator The fitted sklearn estimator (SKLearnProbe) y_true_eval_, y_pred_eval_ ndarray Held-out labels and predictions (SKLearnProbe, holdout and train evaluation) results_ dict Standard detector schema; results_["report"] holds fold_scores, mean_score and std_score under evaluation="cv"

predict(X) returns labels from the fitted estimator or network.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Score Risk level below threshold (0.70) low threshold to 0.85 moderate 0.85 and above high

Baseline correction

With imbalanced groups, compare the score with the majority-class rate: 

baseline = max(np.bincount(probe.y_true_eval_)) / len(probe.y_true_eval_)
corrected = (probe.metric_value_ - baseline) / (1 - baseline)

docs.title: Classifier comparison
docs.text:
Different classifiers pick up different shortcuts:

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

classifiers = {
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
    "Linear SVM": SVC(kernel="linear"),
    "RBF SVM": SVC(kernel="rbf"),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100),
}

for name, clf in classifiers.items():
    probe = SKLearnProbe(clf, metric="accuracy", evaluation="holdout", random_state=42)
    probe.fit(embeddings, group_labels)
    print(f"{name}: {probe.metric_value_:.2%}")
Classifier Best for Logistic Regression Linear shortcuts Linear SVM Margin-based linear separation RBF SVM Non-linear shortcuts Random Forest Complex, non-linear patterns

docs.title: Feature importance
docs.text:
Which dimensions the probe leans on:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

probe = SKLearnProbe(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), metric="accuracy")
probe.fit(embeddings, group_labels)

importance = np.abs(probe.estimator_.coef_).mean(axis=0)
top_features = np.argsort(importance)[-10:]
print("Top 10 shortcut dimensions:", top_features)

With the default estimator (a pipeline), the classifier sits at probe.estimator_.named_steps["clf"].

docs.title: Cross-validation
docs.text:
For a score that depends less on one split:

probe = SKLearnProbe(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), metric="accuracy",
                     evaluation="cv", cv_folds=5, random_state=42)
probe.fit(embeddings, group_labels)

report = probe.get_report()["report"]
print(f"CV accuracy: {report['mean_score']:.2%} (SD {report['std_score']:.2%})")
print(report["fold_scores"])

docs.title: When to use probes
docs.text:
Use probes when:

  • You want a direct measure of how recoverable the group is
  • You need feature importance
  • Your embeddings have many dimensions
  • You want to compare linear and non-linear shortcuts

Don't use probes when:

  • You have very few samples (< 100)
  • Groups are highly imbalanced (correct for the baseline first)
  • You want an unsupervised analysis

docs.title: Theory
docs.text: If the group $G$ can be predicted from the embedding $E$ better than chance, the two share information: $I(E; G) > 0$. A probe's held-out score is one practical reading of that; the paper's audit turns the same idea into a calibrated test by comparing the probe's AUROC with its value under permuted attributes.

docs.text:

docs.title: Shortcut Feature Masking (M01)
docs.text: Shortcut Feature Masking is a data mitigation approach (Teso & Kersting 2019) that produces augmented training data by masking or inpainting detected shortcut regions. Using this data for retraining discourages models from relying on shortcuts.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Teso, S., & Kersting, K. (2019). Explanatory Interactive Machine Learning. AIES 2019. The counterexample strategy randomizes or masks wrongly identified components so the learner does not depend on them.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
• Images: Given images and shortcut regions (from GradCAM heatmaps or user-provided masks), produces new images with those regions zeroed, randomized, or inpainted.
  • Embeddings: Given embeddings and flagged dimension indices (e.g. from HBAC or statistical detection), produces new embeddings with those dimensions zeroed or randomized.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text: Strategy Images Embeddings zero Set shortcut pixels to 0 Set flagged dimensions to 0 randomize Replace shortcut pixels with random values Shuffle values across samples for flagged dims inpaint Fill shortcut regions with mean (simple inpainting) N/A (treated as zero)

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Image mode: NumPy, PIL. No extra dependencies.
  • Embedding mode: NumPy only.

docs.title: Image mode
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutMasker
import numpy as np

masker = ShortcutMasker(strategy="randomize", heatmap_threshold=0.5, augment_fraction=1.0)
# images: (N, H, W) or (N, H, W, C), values in [0, 1]
# shortcut_masks: (N, H, W) binary, or pass heatmaps instead
augmented = masker.mask_images(images, shortcut_masks=masks)
# Or from GradCAM heatmaps:
augmented = masker.mask_images(images, heatmaps=heatmaps)

docs.title: Embedding mode
docs.text:
masker = ShortcutMasker(strategy="zero")
# embeddings: (N, D), flagged_dim_indices: list of dimension indices
augmented = masker.mask_embeddings(embeddings, flagged_dim_indices=[0, 3, 7])

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
In the Advanced Analysis tab, use the Shortcut Feature Masking (M01) accordion:

  • Image mode: Upload images and either mask images or a heatmap file (.npz/.npy). Choose strategy (zero / randomize / inpaint) and augment fraction. Download a zip of augmented images.
  • Embedding mode: Upload an embeddings CSV and enter dimension indices to mask (e.g. 0,3,7). Download the augmented CSV.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Run detection (e.g. GradCAM, HBAC, Statistical) to identify shortcut regions or dimensions.
  2. Run Shortcut Masking with those regions/dimensions to produce augmented data.
  3. Use the augmented data (optionally mixed with original) for retraining.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• strategy: "zero" | "randomize" | "inpaint" (images); "zero" | "randomize" (embeddings).
  • heatmap_threshold: Binarization threshold for heatmaps (default 0.5).
  • augment_fraction: Fraction of samples to augment, 0–1 (default 1.0).
  • random_state: Seed for reproducible randomization.

docs.title: SIS (Sufficient Input Subsets)
docs.text:
Sufficient Input Subsets (SIS) finds minimal subsets of embedding dimensions whose values alone suffice for a black-box predictor to make the same prediction, even when all other dimensions are masked (Carter et al. 2019).

For shortcut detection, small mean SIS size indicates the model may rely on few dimensions to predict, a potential shortcut. If those dimensions overlap with group-discriminative dimensions, the shortcut signal is stronger.

Outside the paper's audit score

This implementation searches for subsets sufficient for the task label, with a fixed subset fraction of 15%, and has no attribute-aware form. It is outside the paper's audit score and contributes to no result there.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
SIS uses instance-wise backward selection:

  1. Train a probe (LogisticRegression) on embeddings → labels
  2. For each test sample: start with full embedding; iteratively mask (zero-out) dimensions in order of least importance (ascending |coef|)
  3. Predict on masked input; if prediction unchanged, keep dimension removed
  4. Report minimal sufficient subset (SIS) per sample
flowchart TB
    subgraph inputs [Inputs]
        E[embeddings]
        L[labels]
        G[group_labels optional]
    end

    subgraph sis [SISDetector]
        P[Train probe on train split]
        B[Backward selection per sample]
        A[Analyze SIS overlap with group]
    end

    E --> P
    L --> P
    P --> B
    E --> B
    L --> B
    B --> A
    G --> A

Shortcut signal: Small mean SIS size (e.g., < 15% of dimensions) or high overlap between SIS dimensions and group-discriminative dimensions.

docs.title: Via the Unified API (Recommended)
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector
import numpy as np

embeddings = np.load("embeddings.npy")
labels = np.load("labels.npy")
group_labels = np.load("groups.npy")  # optional, for group-SIS overlap

detector = ShortcutDetector(methods=["sis"])
detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels=group_labels)

print(detector.summary())
print(detector.results_["sis"]["metrics"]["mean_sis_size"])

docs.title: Standalone Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.xai import SISDetector

detector = SISDetector(
    mask_value=0.0,           # value for masked dimensions
    max_samples=200,         # cap samples for SIS computation
    test_size=0.2,           # train/test split
    shortcut_threshold=0.15,  # frac_dim <= this → shortcut signal
    seed=42,
)
detector.fit(embeddings, labels, group_labels=groups)

metrics = detector.results_["metrics"]
print(metrics["mean_sis_size"], metrics["frac_dimensions"])
print(detector.sis_sizes_)  # per-sample SIS sizes

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description mask_value 0.0 Value used when ablating a dimension max_samples 200 Max test samples for SIS (for performance) test_size 0.2 Fraction for train/test split shortcut_threshold 0.15 If frac_dimensions ≤ this → shortcut signal seed 42 Random seed

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Metric Interpretation Mean SIS size Average number of dimensions sufficient for prediction (smaller = fewer dims used) Fraction of dimensions Mean SIS / n_dim (small = potential shortcut) Group-SIS overlap If group_labels provided: fraction of SIS dims that are group-discriminative (high = shortcut correlates with group)

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Carter, B., Mueller, J., Jain, S., & Gifford, D. (2019). What made you do this? Understanding black-box decisions with sufficient input subsets. Proceedings of the Twenty-Second International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), PMLR 89:567–576.

docs.title: SpRAy (Heatmap Clustering)
docs.text:
SpRAy (Spectral Relevance Analysis) clusters explanation heatmaps to reveal systematic attention patterns that can indicate Clever Hans behavior.

This implementation follows Lapuschkin et al. (2019) and is designed to work with any heatmap generator (e.g., GradCAM). You can provide precomputed heatmaps directly or let SpRAy generate them via a pluggable heatmap generator.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use SpRAy when: - You can compute explanation heatmaps for a set of samples. - You want to discover systematic attention artifacts. - You need an interpretable, cluster-based view of model focus.

Do not use SpRAy when: - You have very few samples (spectral clustering becomes unstable). - Heatmaps are extremely noisy or poorly aligned across samples.

docs.title: Example (Precomputed Heatmaps)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from shortcut_detect import SpRAyDetector

# heatmaps: (N, H, W)
heatmaps = np.load("heatmaps.npy")
labels = np.load("labels.npy")

detector = SpRAyDetector(
    affinity="cosine",
    cluster_selection="auto",
    downsample_size=32,
)
detector.fit(heatmaps=heatmaps, labels=labels)
report = detector.get_report()

print(report["report"]["clever_hans"])

docs.title: Example (Generate Heatmaps via GradCAM)
docs.text:
import torch
from shortcut_detect import SpRAyDetector

model = torch.load("model.pt", map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)
inputs = ...  # tensor of shape (N, C, H, W)

detector = SpRAyDetector(
    affinity="rbf",
    cluster_selection="eigengap",
    max_clusters=8,
)
detector.fit(
    inputs=inputs,
    model=model,
    target_layer="backbone.layer4",
    head="logits",
)
print(detector.summary())

docs.title: Key Outputs
docs.text:
• clusters: size, purity, focus (localization) stats per cluster
  • clever_hans: heuristic flags + risk level
  • representative_heatmaps: mean heatmap per cluster for inspection

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start with affinity="cosine" and cluster_selection="auto".
  • Use downsample_size=32 or 64 to speed up clustering.
  • If you see small, high-purity clusters with very localized attention, investigate corresponding inputs for artifacts.

docs.title: SSA (Spread Spurious Attribute) Detector
docs.text: SSA is a semi-supervised shortcut detection method that pseudo-labels spurious attributes for unlabeled data using a small labeled set, then applies GroupDRO to detect shortcut reliance. It is designed for settings where only a fraction of the data has group annotations.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: SSA operates in two phases:

docs.title: Phase 1: Pseudo-Labeling (Algorithm 1)
docs.text:
1. Split labeled data (DL) into train and validation halves
  2. K-fold split unlabeled data (DU) into K folds
  3. For each fold k:
    • Train an attribute predictor on DL-train + remaining DU folds with adaptive thresholds
    • Predict pseudo spurious-attribute labels for fold k
  4. Adaptive thresholds (Eq. 5-8) balance pseudo-label counts across groups

docs.title: Phase 2: GroupDRO Detection
docs.text:
1. Construct pseudo-groups as (label, pseudo-attribute) pairs
  2. Run GroupDRO on DU with pseudo-groups, validated on DL (true groups)
  3. Detect shortcut if the average-to-worst-group accuracy gap exceeds a threshold
graph TD
    A[DL: Labeled Data] --> B[Split DL into Train/Val]
    C[DU: Unlabeled Data] --> D[K-Fold Split]
    B --> E[Train Attribute Predictor per Fold]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Pseudo-Label Spurious Attributes for DU]
    F --> G[Construct Pseudo-Groups]
    G --> H[GroupDRO on Pseudo-Groups]
    B --> I[Validate on DL True Groups]
    H --> I
    I --> J{Avg - Worst Group Gap >= Threshold?}
    J -->|Yes| K[Shortcut Detected]
    J -->|No| L[No Shortcut Detected]

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect.ssa import SSADetector, SSAConfig

config = SSAConfig(
    K=3,
    T=2000,
    tau_gmin=0.95,
    seed=42,
)

detector = SSADetector(config=config)
detector.fit(
    du_embeddings=unlabeled_embeddings,
    du_labels=unlabeled_labels,
    dl_embeddings=labeled_embeddings,
    dl_labels=labeled_labels,
    dl_spurious=labeled_spurious_attrs,
)

report = detector.get_report()
print(f"Shortcut detected: {report['shortcut_detected']}")
print(f"Risk level: {report['risk_level']}")
print(f"Avg accuracy: {report['metrics']['avg_acc']:.3f}")
print(f"Worst group accuracy: {report['metrics']['worst_group_acc']:.3f}")
print(f"Gap: {report['metrics']['gap']:.3f}")

docs.title: Parameters (SSAConfig)
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description K int 3 Number of K-fold splits for pseudo-labeling T int 2000 Training iterations per fold batch_size int 128 Batch size for training lr float 1e-3 Learning rate for SGD weight_decay float 1e-4 Weight decay for SGD momentum float 0.9 SGD momentum hidden_dim int or None None Hidden layer size for attribute predictor (None = linear) dropout float 0.0 Dropout rate for attribute predictor tau_gmin float 0.95 Confidence threshold for the smallest group threshold_update_every int 200 How often to update adaptive thresholds dl_val_fraction float 0.5 Fraction of DL used for validation seed int 0 Random seed device str or None None PyTorch device (auto-detected if None) groupdro GroupDROConfig default Configuration for the Phase 2 GroupDRO ssa_gap_threshold float 0.10 Accuracy gap threshold for shortcut detection

docs.title: Report Structure
docs.text: Field Type Description shortcut_detected bool or None Whether the accuracy gap exceeds the threshold risk_level str "low", "moderate", or "unknown" metrics.n_labeled int Number of labeled (DL) samples metrics.n_unlabeled int Number of unlabeled (DU) samples metrics.avg_acc float Average accuracy from GroupDRO metrics.worst_group_acc float Worst-group accuracy from GroupDRO metrics.gap float Average minus worst-group accuracy

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Risk Level Condition Low Accuracy gap < threshold (no shortcut detected) Moderate Accuracy gap >= threshold (shortcut detected) Unknown Insufficient data or non-finite metrics

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Use SSA when:

  • You have a small set of group-labeled data and a larger unlabeled set
  • You suspect spurious correlations but lack complete group annotations
  • You want to leverage semi-supervised learning for shortcut detection
  • Your data has both task labels and (partial) spurious attribute labels

Don't use SSA when:

  • You have complete group labels for all data (use GroupDRO directly)
  • You have no group labels at all (use GCE or Probe-based detection)
  • Your dataset is very small (SSA needs enough data for K-fold splitting)
  • You cannot use PyTorch (SSA requires torch for training)

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
SSA (Spread Spurious Attribute) addresses the realistic scenario where group annotations are expensive and only available for a small subset. The key insight is that a pseudo-labeler trained on a mix of labeled and high-confidence unlabeled data can propagate spurious attribute labels to the full dataset.

Adaptive thresholds (Eq. 5-8) ensure balanced pseudo-label counts across groups by setting per-group confidence thresholds relative to the smallest group:

$$g_{\min} = \arg\min_g |D_L^{\circ}(g)|$$

The threshold for each group is chosen so that the total (labeled + pseudo-labeled) count per group does not exceed a cap derived from $g_{\min}$.

After pseudo-labeling, GroupDRO optimizes worst-group performance. A large gap between average and worst-group accuracy indicates that the model relies on spurious correlations (shortcuts).

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• GroupDRO - The robust training method used in Phase 2
  • Demographic Parity - Group-level fairness metric
  • API Reference - Full API documentation
  • Overview - Compare all methods

docs.title: Statistical testing
docs.text: Statistical testing finds the embedding dimensions along which the groups differ. It is the one method that names specific dimensions.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. For every dimension, GroupDiffTest runs a two-sample test between the groups (Mann-Whitney U in the pipeline; any SciPy-style test works)
  2. With two groups there is one comparison; with three or more, every one-vs-one and one-vs-rest comparison
  3. apply_correction adjusts the p-values of each comparison for multiple testing (Benjamini-Hochberg by default) and lists the dimensions that stay significant
  4. A comparison with at least one significant dimension sets shortcut_detected_
graph TD
    A[Embeddings] --> B[Split by group]
    B --> C[Dimension 1]
    B --> D[Dimension 2]
    B --> E[...]
    B --> F[Dimension N]
    C --> G[Two-sample test]
    D --> G
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[P-values per comparison]
    H --> I[Multiple testing correction]
    I --> J[Significant dimensions]

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu
from shortcut_detect import GroupDiffTest

test = GroupDiffTest(test=mannwhitneyu)
test.fit(embeddings, group_labels)

raw = test.get_pvalues()   # {comparison: array of p-values, one per dimension}
corrected = test.apply_correction(alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh", verbose=False)

for comparison, significant in corrected["significant_features"].items():
    print(f"{comparison}: {len(significant or [])} significant dimensions")
print(test.shortcut_detected_)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
GroupDiffTest(test, **test_kwargs), an alias of FeatureGroupDiffTest:

Parameter Type Description test callable Called as test(x1, x2, **test_kwargs) on the two groups' values of one dimension. Must return a p-value, or a tuple whose second element is the p-value (SciPy's convention) **test_kwargs Forwarded to test, for example alternative="two-sided"

The significance level and the correction are arguments of apply_threshold and apply_correction, not of the constructor.

docs.title: Available tests
docs.text:
Each call sees exactly two samples (one dimension, two groups), so any SciPy two-sample test fits:

from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu, ttest_ind, ks_2samp

test = GroupDiffTest(test=mannwhitneyu)   # rank-based, no normality assumption
test = GroupDiffTest(test=ttest_ind)      # assumes normality
test = GroupDiffTest(test=ks_2samp)       # any difference in distribution
test = GroupDiffTest(test=mannwhitneyu, alternative="greater")  # kwargs reach the test

With three or more groups the class runs every one-vs-one and one-vs-rest comparison with the same two-sample test; there is no need for a k-sample test.

docs.title: Multiple testing correction
docs.text:
test.fit(embeddings, group_labels)

bh = test.apply_correction(alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh", verbose=False)        # Benjamini-Hochberg
bonferroni = test.apply_correction(alpha=0.05, method="bonferroni", verbose=False)
holm = test.apply_correction(alpha=0.05, method="holm", verbose=False)
by = test.apply_correction(alpha=0.05, method="fdr_by", verbose=False)        # Benjamini-Yekutieli

uncorrected = test.apply_threshold(alpha=0.05, verbose=False)  # raw p < alpha, not recommended
Method Controls Strictness bonferroni family-wise error rate strictest holm family-wise error rate strict fdr_bh false discovery rate moderate (default in the pipeline) fdr_by false discovery rate under dependence between holm and fdr_bh

Each apply_correction call returns a dict with significant_features, corrected_pvalues and rejected (all keyed by comparison), plus method and alpha, and updates shortcut_detected_ and results_.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Name Type Description p_values_ dict Raw p-values per comparison (array of length embedding_dim); also returned by get_pvalues() shortcut_detected_ bool or None None after fit; set by apply_threshold or apply_correction apply_correction(...)["corrected_pvalues"] dict Adjusted p-values per comparison apply_correction(...)["significant_features"] dict Significant dimension indices per comparison, or None when there are none apply_correction(...)["rejected"] dict Boolean mask per comparison

The class computes no effect sizes; see Effect size calculation for a few lines that do.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
% significant dimensions Reading < 5% Few dimensions carry group information 5-20% Some dimensions carry it 20-50% Many dimensions carry it > 50% Group information is spread through the embedding

These bands are a reading aid, not a decision rule. The paper's audit uses the fraction of BH-significant dimensions within task strata as one secondary statistic and calibrates it against a permutation null; see the Audit API.

docs.title: Volcano plot
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

comparison = next(iter(corrected["corrected_pvalues"]))
q = corrected["corrected_pvalues"][comparison]
significant = set(corrected["significant_features"][comparison] or [])

# Cohen's d per dimension, computed by hand
g0, g1 = np.unique(group_labels)[:2]
x0, x1 = embeddings[group_labels == g0], embeddings[group_labels == g1]
pooled = np.sqrt((x0.var(axis=0, ddof=1) + x1.var(axis=0, ddof=1)) / 2)
d = (x1.mean(axis=0) - x0.mean(axis=0)) / pooled

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
colors = ["red" if i in significant else "gray" for i in range(len(d))]
ax.scatter(d, -np.log10(q + 1e-300), c=colors, alpha=0.5)
ax.axhline(-np.log10(0.05), color="blue", linestyle="--", label="q = 0.05")
ax.set_xlabel("Cohen's d")
ax.set_ylabel("-log10(BH-adjusted p)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("volcano_plot.png")

docs.title: Most significant dimensions
docs.text:
order = np.argsort(q)[:20]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
ax.barh(range(len(order)), -np.log10(q[order] + 1e-300))
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order)))
ax.set_yticklabels([f"dim {i}" for i in order])
ax.set_xlabel("-log10(BH-adjusted p)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("significant_features.png")

docs.title: Effect size calculation
docs.text:
P-values say whether a dimension differs; an effect size says by how much:

def cohens_d(group1, group2):
    n1, n2 = len(group1), len(group2)
    var1, var2 = group1.var(ddof=1), group2.var(ddof=1)
    pooled_std = np.sqrt(((n1 - 1) * var1 + (n2 - 1) * var2) / (n1 + n2 - 2))
    return (group1.mean() - group2.mean()) / pooled_std

effect_sizes = np.array([
    cohens_d(embeddings[group_labels == g0, dim], embeddings[group_labels == g1, dim])
    for dim in range(embeddings.shape[1])
])

| Effect size (|d|) | Interpretation | |-------------------|----------------| | < 0.2 | Small | | 0.2 - 0.5 | Medium | | 0.5 - 0.8 | Large | | > 0.8 | Very large |

docs.title: Several groups
docs.text:
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu

test = GroupDiffTest(test=mannwhitneyu)
test.fit(embeddings, group_labels)   # labels 0, 1, 2, ...
corrected = test.apply_correction(alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh", verbose=False)

for comparison, significant in corrected["significant_features"].items():
    # keys such as 0_vs_1, 0_vs_2, 1_vs_2, 0_vs_rest, 1_vs_rest, 2_vs_rest
    print(f"{comparison}: {len(significant or [])} significant dimensions")

docs.title: When to use statistical testing
docs.text:
Use statistical testing when:

  • You want to identify specific biased dimensions
  • You need interpretable, dimension-level results
  • Your embeddings are high-dimensional

Don't use statistical testing when:

  • Biases are non-linear or interaction-based
  • You have very few samples per group
  • You only care about aggregate shortcut presence

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
For each dimension $d$ the null hypothesis is that its distribution is the same across groups, and $p_d$ is the probability of the observed difference under that null.

Multiple testing correction controls the false discovery rate:

$$\text{FDR} = E\left[\frac{\text{False Positives}}{\text{Total Rejections}}\right] \leq \alpha$$

docs.title: VAE (Variational Autoencoder) Shortcut Detection
docs.text: VAE-based shortcut detection (Müller et al., Fraunhofer-AISEC) uses Beta-VAE disentanglement to identify latent dimensions with high predictiveness for the target label.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• torch and torchvision (included in core install; see Installation)

Reference: Müller et al., "Shortcut Detection with Variational Autoencoders", ICML 2023 Workshop on Spurious Correlations, Invariance and Stability. GitHub

docs.title: What It Detects
docs.text:
• Latent dimensions that are highly predictive of the target label (classifier weights).
  • High predictiveness indicates the dimension may encode a shortcut (spurious correlation).

docs.title: Required Inputs
docs.text:
• images: np.ndarray or torch.Tensor (N, C, H, W) or (N, H, W, C)
  • labels: np.ndarray (N,) class labels
  • img_size: int, image height/width (assume square)

Or provide DataLoaders instead:

  • train_dl, val_dl: PyTorch DataLoaders
  • test_dl: optional, for latent extraction (defaults to val_dl)
  • img_size, channels, num_classes

docs.title: Optional Inputs
docs.text:
• channels: default 3 (RGB)
  • num_classes: default 2
  • vae_checkpoint: path to pre-trained VAE (skip training)
  • device: "cuda:0" or "cpu"

docs.title: Unified API Example
docs.text:
from shortcut_detect import ShortcutDetector
import torch

# Using numpy/tensor arrays
images = torch.randn(200, 3, 64, 64)  # or np.ndarray
labels = (torch.rand(200) > 0.5).long().numpy()

bundle = {
    "images": images,
    "labels": labels,
    "img_size": 64,
    "channels": 3,
    "num_classes": 2,
}

detector = ShortcutDetector(
    methods=["vae"],
    vae_latent_dim=10,
    vae_kld_weight=3.0,
    vae_epochs=50,
)
detector.fit_from_loaders({"vae": bundle})

result = detector.get_results()["vae"]
print(result["metrics"])
print(result["report"]["per_dimension"])

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• Predictiveness: Sum of absolute classifier weights per latent dimension. High values indicate the dimension is used for classification (candidate shortcut).
  • MPWD (max pairwise Wasserstein distance): Class separability per dimension.
  • Flagged: Dimensions where normalized predictiveness exceeds the threshold (default 0.5).
  • Risk levels:
  • high: many dimensions flagged (≥ half of latent dims)
  • moderate: at least one dimension flagged
  • low: no dimensions flagged

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Müller, Nicolas M., Simon Roschmann, Shahbaz Khan, Philip Sperl, and Konstantin Böttinger. "Shortcut Detection with Variational Autoencoders." ICML 2023 Workshop on Spurious Correlations, Invariance and Stability.

docs.title: Playwright E2E Tests
docs.text: End-to-end tests for the Gradio dashboard using Playwright.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[e2e]"
playwright install chromium

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
Option 1: Dashboard already running

# In one terminal:
GRADIO_SERVER_PORT=7860 python app.py

# In another:
GRADIO_TEST_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7860 pytest tests/e2e/ -v -m e2e

Option 2: Auto-start dashboard

pytest tests/e2e/ -v -m e2e

The conftest will start the dashboard if it is not already running at http://127.0.0.1:7860.
